p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> By one measure (https://nlihc.org/gap/state/ca), California is short nearly 1.4 million homes for people earning very low incomes. At the same time, middle-income families also struggle to afford housing in the state, where single-family homes sold for a median price (https://www.car.org/marketdata/data/countysalesactivity) of $887,680 in July.
In response, lawmakers are asking voters to let the state borrow $11.25 billion through the sale of bonds to build and maintain housing that low- and middle-income residents can afford.
It’s called Proposition 1, or the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026.

What will the measure do?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> The largest chunk of this money — $7.2 billion — would be doled out as loans to builders who agree to rent some of the homes to low-income families; in Los Angeles County, a family of four earning about $133,000 a year qualifies as low-income.
Advertisement
Researchers recently found (https://www.enterprisecommunity.org/sites/default/files/2026-03/2026_State_Pipeline_Brief.pdf) that the construction of nearly 40,000 low-income homes was in limbo because of a lack of funding.
The second-largest portion of these funds — $1.25 billion — would be set aside for housing for veterans, in the form of homeownership loans. Voters last approved this type of statewide bond for veteran home loans in 2018.
According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf), the remaining dollars would be spread across several other initiatives and could subsidize up to 40,000 rental apartments, 2,500 homes for farmworkers and 1,200 beds for university students:
$1.1 billion to help low- and middle-income families buy homes through direct loans and funds to nonprofits
$500 million for infrastructure related to new housing, such as road and water repairs
$450 million in loans or grants to build or upkeep affordable housing for farmworkers
$350 million to build affordable housing for students, split evenly among the University of California and California State University
$200 million available for tribal members to use to build or repair housing
$200 million available to city and county governments and other entities hoping to pilot programs to build low-cost housing

Who are the supporters?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> When lawmakers voted to put this funding on the ballot this year, the votes were split almost entirely among party lines, with state Democrats in support.

“Through this historic bond, we’re giving voters the opportunity to help more Californians achieve homeownership, expand access to affordable housing, and give more families a real shot at the California Dream,” Gov. Gavin Newsom said about the proposition in June.
The bill to put this item on the ballot also was widely supported by organizations that provide low-income housing, plus various municipal governments, including San Diego, Orange and Santa Barbara counties.
Who are the opponents?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Republicans, who represented all of the votes against Proposition 1, said on the legislative floor that the state instead should curtail building regulations to bring down the cost of housing without burdening taxpayers.
“We know the cost of building in California is extraordinarily, exponentially higher than it needs to be,” said Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, a Republican who represents cities and towns just east of San Diego. “We need reforms first before we take out the credit card and borrow money.”
Why is this on the ballot?

Here’s what $44 billion would buy by Mikhail Zinshteyn (https://calmatters.org/author/mikhailzinshteyn/) October 24, 2026 Updated October 25, 2026 Republish Share this: Share on X (Opens in new window) X (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/bond-measures-on-california-ballot/) Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/bond-measures-on-california-ballot/) Share on WhatsApp (Opens in new window) WhatsApp (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/bond-measures-on-california-ballot/) Construction in a residential area that was burned during the Eaton Fire in 2025, in Altadena, on Aug. 3, 2026. Photo by Jules Hotz for CalMatters In summary Californians will decide on $44 billion in bonds when the vote on Propositions 1, 37 and 38. They’d take out debt to pay for housing and medical research. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. Your November ballot is welcoming you to make it rain … in bonds. You’ll see an El Nino-sized set of propositions that could flood the housing construction and science research components of the California economy with $44 billion of bond spending if the measures pass. Two of those bond proposals — Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/) for housing and Proposition 38 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) for immunology research — are the traditional borrow-now, pay-back-later arrangements that add a few billion dollars to the overall cost of the propositions. A third, Proposition 37 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/), is an atypical measure that amounts to a low-risk radical experiment that taxpayers likely won’t be on the hook for, at least not directly. Historically, bond propositions win the approval of voters at higher rates than other measures. Since 2000, voters passed 23 of the 26 statewide bonds before them, an 88% yay rate. In recent years voters approved billions in bond debt for school construction, combatting the effects of climate change and housing for veterans. Bonds are a form of debt that the state must pay off over time, and that means annual payments with interest (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/voter-info/overview-state-bond-debt.htm). The state spends $6 billion annually to repay about $80 billion of bonds. Voters and lawmakers have also approved $40 billion in bonds that have yet to be sold. Fortunately for your ballot studying, the following cheat sheet is a primer on just the three bonds before you. Prop. 1: Affordable housing If voters say yes, Prop. 1 would permit California’s treasurer (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/) to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds. That money would provide various types of housing, including to veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes. The measure dedicates $7 billion to constructing, refurbishing, or acquiring apartment complexes, primarily through loans to developers of affordable housing. These developments must serve low-income residents, reserving at least 10% of units for extremely low-income households. Over $1 billion of this total supports permanent and interim housing for the homeless. The bond, if passed, would result in some 40,000 new rental units, wrote (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) the Legislative Analyst’s Office, which is the nonpartisan think-tank of the Legislature. This is the only bond measure on the ballot put forward by lawmakers. The other two secured enough signatures from voters to secure a spot for the November election. Opposition to this bond is minimal. The state Republican Party’s officially neutral on the measure. Several Republican lawmakers in June voted no on the bill that metamorphosed into this bond. They argued that the bill’s title — The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb417) — misled the public on just how much of the bond revenue would support veterans. The answer? $1.25 billion for veterans to secure home loans. Another $350 million would head to the state’s two public university systems to help finance the development of student dorms. But with costs per bed often exceeding $250,000, all those tens of millions of dollars would secure dorms for around 1,300 students. Just the right amount of news Just the right amount of news Get California’s most essential headlines without feeling overwhelmed. Get California’s most essential headlines without feeling overwhelmed. Email address By clicking subscribe, you agree to the terms (https://calmatters.org/about/policies-and-standards/). Sign up for free Δ Support for Prop. 1 is vast, including Gov. Gavin Newsom, the state Democratic party, home-sharing company AirBnB, major unions and more. Want more? Read CalMatters’ Marisa Kendall’s guide to Prop. 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/). Prop. 37: Help for down payments This bond measure is strange (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-37-homebuyers-loan/), novel and introduces a bevy of unknowns. Confused? So is everyone else, which is why CalMatters’ housing reporter Ben Christopher described this unorthodox proposition as “plainly weird.” (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/) Prop. 37 should be viewed as a way to help buyers of new homes secure down payments. The language permits individuals to apply for as much as 17% of the purchase price of a new house, condo or townhome. That covers much of the typical 20% down payment. Who’s eligible? Roughly 90% of all California renters. The income caps vary by county, so around $115,000 in Imperial and north of $400,000 in San Mateo for a family of three. Eligible homes must satisfy several conditions: They’re new or newly converted and don’t cost more than roughly $1.5 million in the Bay Area or $1 million in Riverside — again, it’s based on a weedy formula by county. What won’t it do? Add to the state’s debt repayment log. This is not a bond that taxpayers will pay back; instead private lenders who provide this bond money will be repaid by homebuyers in the form of interest payments. How many homes this could buy is impossible to predict. That number depends on how much the new homes cost, the incomes of the homebuyers and whether developers build new homes. Most renters today couldn’t afford even the cheapest new homes, said Eric McGhee, an analyst for the nonprofit Public Policy Institute of California who’s written about Prop. 37 (https://www.ppic.org/blog/how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37/). He estimated that anywhere from 60,000 to more than 1.8 million buyers could take advantage of the down payment assistance through this bond measure. The lower end assumes a 20% down payment on the most expensive homes. The higher end assumes 5% down payments on the least expensive homes. Prop. 38: Immunology research This bond proposal (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-38-research-bond/) would commit $4.2 billion to a single, unnamed nonprofit institute that focuses on immunology research and cures for major diseases such as Alzheimer’s, cancer and heart disease. The same amount would be distributed to a committee that’d identify a limited number of researchers at public universities and nonprofits who study immunology and immunotherapies. Previous reporting by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) found only one institute in California currently meets Prop. 38’s criteria for half of the money: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The institute’s primary funder is billionaire Gary K. Michelson, who wrote Prop. 38 and is by far the largest donor to its political campaign. Additional CalMatters reporting raises the question of how ready is the institute to implement the bond’s vast dollars. The institute had only three employees (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) as of last month, far fewer than the 51 it planned to have on staff last year. The Yes on 38 campaign says the bond revenue is needed to hedge against the Trump administration’s ongoing efforts to cut federal science research or limit what’s studied. They argue that any curtailment of drug trials and other therapies can lead to avoidable pain and death for patients of debilitating maladies. Opponents of the measure fault it for concentrating half the money in a single institute and limiting which other researchers can receive the funding. They say science research is best performed in a competitive environment that’s open to all of California’s nonprofit and public university scientists. The problem underlying California’s housing crisis comes down to this: the cost of construction.
It constrains new supply. And the only way to recoup the costs of what does get built requires high rents and mortgages or — in the case of affordable housing — public subsidies.
Unfortunately, the solution to this crisis offered by two statewide propositions has nothing to do with addressing prohibitive building costs. Instead, their answer is to load Californians with debt while delivering bonanzas to home developers and builders.

Proposition 1 leaves taxpayers indebted; Proposition 37, homebuyers.
Reject both.
Proposition 1
This measure, placed on the ballot by the state Legislature through Senate Bill 407, is an expensive pandering potpourri of giveaways. Veterans, farmworkers, students, tribes are all the ostensible beneficiaries.
Here’s how it is supposed to work:
Proposition 1 would authorize the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds, all earmarked for various housing programs. The bulk of the bonds, $7.2 billion, would be spent acquiring, building or renovating apartments. The backers of this proposition optimistically estimate that it would subsidize the construction of “up to” 40,000 multifamily rental units as well as 2,500 housing units for farmworkers and 1,200 beds for university students.
Another $1.1 billion would provide homeownership assistance for 40,000 families. The remainder of funds would go toward infrastructure projects ($500 million), farmworker housing ($450 million), student housing at the UC and Cal State systems ($350 million), and tribal housing ($200 million).
Additionally, $1.25 billion would be dedicated to home loan assistance for veterans. (This program is not expected to create direct costs as participating veterans would pay monthly payments to the state, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office.)
The need for affordable housing and housing assistance in this state is undeniable. More than two in five households spend, at least, 30% of their incomes on housing.
However, Proposition 1 would only provide a drop in the bucket towards adding to the state’s housing supply, all while hamstringing state spending and burdening taxpayers with decades of debt. The LAO projects that paying off $10 billion in bond debt incurred by this measure would require annual payments between $500 million to $600 million for a quarter of a century. These payments would come from California’s checking account, the General Fund. Because the state has to pay interest on the money it borrows, per the LAO, the total cost of the bond would be about 15% more (after adjusting for inflation) than if the state paid up front with money it already has.
Perhaps that would be acceptable if this burst of spending would make a long-term difference, but it’s doubtful.
Consider that California needs to build 2.5 million new homes, including 1 million affordable ones, to keep up with demand.
But this measure would add only 4% toward the affordable total, and that’s only under pie-in-the-sky circumstances.
More disconcerting is how this measure would do nothing to attack the root of the affordable housing cost problem:
Building subsidized housing in California costs 1.5 times the average cost of building already-exorbitant market-rate housing here, according to a 2025 RAND study.
The nonpartisan think tank identified two major reasons for the discrepancy: Local governments charge “unusually large” architectural and engineering fees, and they require that affordable housing developers pay “substantially above-market” wages.
While $200 million of Proposition 1 would go toward “pilot” programs aimed at developing reduced housing models, at least $10 billion would be spent keeping this bloated model afloat.
Proposition 37
This measure looks great on the surface. It would help Californians buy new homes, all without costing taxpayers a dime.
Well, all that glitters isn’t gold.
Proposition 37 would authorize up to $25 billion in revenue bonds for downpayment assistance on newly constructed homes. Eligible buyers could borrow up to 17% of a home’s purchase price through a fixed-rate second mortgage, making a down payment as low as 3%.
For example, consider an $800,000 home. A buyer could put down $24,000, borrow $136,000 through Proposition 37 and then finance the remaining $640,000 using a conventional mortgage.
A 30-year loan at today’s rates would make the monthly costs of that second mortgage more than $900.
Proposition 37 is not reducing the burden of home prices in California.
It’s not solving the affordability crisis.
It’s just a creative way to help Californians take on more debt.
What rightly worries critics is the terms of these additional loans. When borrowers default, the primary mortgage lender gets repaid first, meaning that the owner of the secondary takes on more risk. That would almost certainly mean that investors would require that buyers pay higher rates on their second mortgages than they pay on the first.
The LAO identifies these financing terms and investor participation as significant uncertainties.
Proposition 37 does nothing to address the main obstacle to homeownership in the state: the monthly cost of a conventional mortgage.
While the majority of renters in the state have incomes that would make them eligible to benefit from the measure’s secondary mortgage program, many wouldn’t qualify for a conventional mortgage in the first place even with its down payment assistance, according to the Public Policy Institute of California.
Far from solving the problem of high home prices, Proposition 37 could compound it.
While the measure restricts using the downpayment assistance to previously unpurchased homes, that does not mean that Proposition 37 will unleash a large new supply of housing.
What’s infinitely more probable is that Proposition 37 would expand purchasing power faster than it would induce new construction — and therefore push up prices.
Homes in California, especially new ones, are sitting unsold longer. In fact, builders have created a glut of new housing in the Central Valley they can’t sell, a dynamic exacerbated as interest rates have climbed. They’d take out debt to pay for housing and medical research. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. Your November ballot is welcoming you to make it rain … in bonds. You’ll see an El Nino-sized set of propositions that could flood the housing construction and science research components of the California economy with $44 billion of bond spending if the measures pass. Two of those bond proposals — Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/) for housing and Proposition 38 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) for immunology research — are the traditional borrow-now, pay-back-later arrangements that add a few billion dollars to the overall cost of the propositions. A third, Proposition 37 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/), is an atypical measure that amounts to a low-risk radical experiment that taxpayers likely won’t be on the hook for, at least not directly. Historically, bond propositions win the approval of voters at higher rates than other measures. Since 2000, voters passed 23 of the 26 statewide bonds before them, an 88% yay rate. In recent years voters approved billions in bond debt for school construction, combatting the effects of climate change and housing for veterans. Bonds are a form of debt that the state must pay off over time, and that means annual payments with interest (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/voter-info/overview-state-bond-debt.htm). The state spends $6 billion annually to repay about $80 billion of bonds. Voters and lawmakers have also approved $40 billion in bonds that have yet to be sold. Fortunately for your ballot studying, the following cheat sheet is a primer on just the three bonds before you. Prop. 1: Affordable housing If voters say yes, Prop. 1 would permit California’s treasurer (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/) to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds. That money would provide various types of housing, including to veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes. The measure dedicates $7 billion to constructing, refurbishing, or acquiring apartment complexes, primarily through loans to developers of affordable housing. These developments must serve low-income residents, reserving at least 10% of units for extremely low-income households. Over $1 billion of this total supports permanent and interim housing for the homeless. The bond, if passed, would result in some 40,000 new rental units, wrote (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) the Legislative Analyst’s Office, which is the nonpartisan think-tank of the Legislature. This is the only bond measure on the ballot put forward by lawmakers. The other two secured enough signatures from voters to secure a spot for the November election. Opposition to this bond is minimal. The state Republican Party’s officially neutral on the measure. Several Republican lawmakers in June voted no on the bill that metamorphosed into this bond. They argued that the bill’s title — The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb417) — misled the public on just how much of the bond revenue would support veterans. The answer? $1.25 billion for veterans to secure home loans. Another $350 million would head to the state’s two public university systems to help finance the development of student dorms. But with costs per bed often exceeding $250,000, all those tens of millions of dollars would secure dorms for around 1,300 students. Read CalMatters’ Marisa Kendall’s guide to Prop. 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/). Prop. 37: Help for down payments This bond measure is strange (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-37-homebuyers-loan/), novel and introduces a bevy of unknowns. Confused? So is everyone else, which is why CalMatters’ housing reporter Ben Christopher described this unorthodox proposition as “plainly weird.” (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/) Prop. 37 should be viewed as a way to help buyers of new homes secure down payments. The language permits individuals to apply for as much as 17% of the purchase price of a new house, condo or townhome. That covers much of the typical 20% down payment. Who’s eligible? Roughly 90% of all California renters. The income caps vary by county, so around $115,000 in Imperial and north of $400,000 in San Mateo for a family of three. Eligible homes must satisfy several conditions: They’re new or newly converted and don’t cost more than roughly $1.5 million in the Bay Area or $1 million in Riverside — again, it’s based on a weedy formula by county. What won’t it do? Add to the state’s debt repayment log. This is not a bond that taxpayers will pay back; instead private lenders who provide this bond money will be repaid by homebuyers in the form of interest payments. How many homes this could buy is impossible to predict. That number depends on how much the new homes cost, the incomes of the homebuyers and whether developers build new homes. Most renters today couldn’t afford even the cheapest new homes, said Eric McGhee, an analyst for the nonprofit Public Policy Institute of California who’s written about Prop. 37 (https://www.ppic.org/blog/how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37/). He estimated that anywhere from 60,000 to more than 1.8 million buyers could take advantage of the down payment assistance through this bond measure. The lower end assumes a 20% down payment on the most expensive homes. The higher end assumes 5% down payments on the least expensive homes. Prop. 38: Immunology research This bond proposal (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-38-research-bond/) would commit $4.2 billion to a single, unnamed nonprofit institute that focuses on immunology research and cures for major diseases such as Alzheimer’s, cancer and heart disease. The same amount would be distributed to a committee that’d identify a limited number of researchers at public universities and nonprofits who study immunology and immunotherapies. Previous reporting by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) found only one institute in California currently meets Prop. 38’s criteria for half of the money: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The institute’s primary funder is billionaire Gary K. Michelson, who wrote Prop. 38 and is by far the largest donor to its political campaign. Additional CalMatters reporting raises the question of how ready is the institute to implement the bond’s vast dollars. The institute had only three employees (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) as of last month, far fewer than the 51 it planned to have on staff last year. The Yes on 38 campaign says the bond revenue is needed to hedge against the Trump administration’s ongoing efforts to cut federal science research or limit what’s studied. They argue that any curtailment of drug trials and other therapies can lead to avoidable pain and death for patients of debilitating maladies. Opponents of the measure fault it for concentrating half the money in a single institute and limiting which other researchers can receive the funding. They say science research is best performed in a competitive environment that’s open to all of California’s nonprofit and public university scientists. The problem underlying California’s housing crisis comes down to this: the cost of construction.
It constrains new supply. And the only way to recoup the costs of what does get built requires high rents and mortgages or — in the case of affordable housing — public subsidies.
Unfortunately, the solution to this crisis offered by two statewide propositions has nothing to do with addressing prohibitive building costs. Instead, their answer is to load Californians with debt while delivering bonanzas to home developers and builders.

Proposition 1 leaves taxpayers indebted; Proposition 37, homebuyers.
Reject both.
Proposition 1
This measure, placed on the ballot by the state Legislature through Senate Bill 407, is an expensive pandering potpourri of giveaways. Veterans, farmworkers, students, tribes are all the ostensible beneficiaries.
Here’s how it is supposed to work:
Proposition 1 would authorize the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds, all earmarked for various housing programs. The bulk of the bonds, $7.2 billion, would be spent acquiring, building or renovating apartments. The backers of this proposition optimistically estimate that it would subsidize the construction of “up to” 40,000 multifamily rental units as well as 2,500 housing units for farmworkers and 1,200 beds for university students.
Another $1.1 billion would provide homeownership assistance for 40,000 families. The remainder of funds would go toward infrastructure projects ($500 million), farmworker housing ($450 million), student housing at the UC and Cal State systems ($350 million), and tribal housing ($200 million).
Additionally, $1.25 billion would be dedicated to home loan assistance for veterans. (This program is not expected to create direct costs as participating veterans would pay monthly payments to the state, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office.)
The need for affordable housing and housing assistance in this state is undeniable. More than two in five households spend, at least, 30% of their incomes on housing.
However, Proposition 1 would only provide a drop in the bucket towards adding to the state’s housing supply, all while hamstringing state spending and burdening taxpayers with decades of debt. The LAO projects that paying off $10 billion in bond debt incurred by this measure would require annual payments between $500 million to $600 million for a quarter of a century. These payments would come from California’s checking account, the General Fund. Because the state has to pay interest on the money it borrows, per the LAO, the total cost of the bond would be about 15% more (after adjusting for inflation) than if the state paid up front with money it already has.
Perhaps that would be acceptable if this burst of spending would make a long-term difference, but it’s doubtful.
Consider that California needs to build 2.5 million new homes, including 1 million affordable ones, to keep up with demand.
But this measure would add only 4% toward the affordable total, and that’s only under pie-in-the-sky circumstances.
More disconcerting is how this measure would do nothing to attack the root of the affordable housing cost problem:
Building subsidized housing in California costs 1.5 times the average cost of building already-exorbitant market-rate housing here, according to a 2025 RAND study.
The nonpartisan think tank identified two major reasons for the discrepancy: Local governments charge “unusually large” architectural and engineering fees, and they require that affordable housing developers pay “substantially above-market” wages.
While $200 million of Proposition 1 would go toward “pilot” programs aimed at developing reduced housing models, at least $10 billion would be spent keeping this bloated model afloat.
Proposition 37
This measure looks great on the surface. It would help Californians buy new homes, all without costing taxpayers a dime.
Well, all that glitters isn’t gold.
Proposition 37 would authorize up to $25 billion in revenue bonds for downpayment assistance on newly constructed homes. Eligible buyers could borrow up to 17% of a home’s purchase price through a fixed-rate second mortgage, making a down payment as low as 3%.
For example, consider an $800,000 home. A buyer could put down $24,000, borrow $136,000 through Proposition 37 and then finance the remaining $640,000 using a conventional mortgage.
A 30-year loan at today’s rates would make the monthly costs of that second mortgage more than $900.
Proposition 37 is not reducing the burden of home prices in California.
It’s not solving the affordability crisis.
It’s just a creative way to help Californians take on more debt.
What rightly worries critics is the terms of these additional loans. When borrowers default, the primary mortgage lender gets repaid first, meaning that the owner of the secondary takes on more risk. That would almost certainly mean that investors would require that buyers pay higher rates on their second mortgages than they pay on the first.
The LAO identifies these financing terms and investor participation as significant uncertainties.
Proposition 37 does nothing to address the main obstacle to homeownership in the state: the monthly cost of a conventional mortgage.
While the majority of renters in the state have incomes that would make them eligible to benefit from the measure’s secondary mortgage program, many wouldn’t qualify for a conventional mortgage in the first place even with its down payment assistance, according to the Public Policy Institute of California.
Far from solving the problem of high home prices, Proposition 37 could compound it.
While the measure restricts using the downpayment assistance to previously unpurchased homes, that does not mean that Proposition 37 will unleash a large new supply of housing.
What’s infinitely more probable is that Proposition 37 would expand purchasing power faster than it would induce new construction — and therefore push up prices.
Homes in California, especially new ones, are sitting unsold longer. In fact, builders have created a glut of new housing in the Central Valley they can’t sell, a dynamic exacerbated as interest rates have climbed. In fact, this summer Fresno topped Realtor.com’s list of U.S. cities with the highest share of new home listings (68%) cutting prices. The problem underlying California’s housing crisis comes down to this: the cost of construction.
It constrains new supply. And the only way to recoup the costs of what does get built requires high rents and mortgages or — in the case of affordable housing — public subsidies.
Unfortunately, the solution to this crisis offered by two statewide propositions has nothing to do with addressing prohibitive building costs. Instead, their answer is to load Californians with debt while delivering bonanzas to home developers and builders.

Proposition 1 leaves taxpayers indebted; Proposition 37, homebuyers.
Reject both.
Proposition 1
This measure, placed on the ballot by the state Legislature through Senate Bill 407, is an expensive pandering potpourri of giveaways. Veterans, farmworkers, students, tribes are all the ostensible beneficiaries.
Here’s how it is supposed to work:
Proposition 1 would authorize the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds, all earmarked for various housing programs. The bulk of the bonds, $7.2 billion, would be spent acquiring, building or renovating apartments. The backers of this proposition optimistically estimate that it would subsidize the construction of “up to” 40,000 multifamily rental units as well as 2,500 housing units for farmworkers and 1,200 beds for university students.
Another $1.1 billion would provide homeownership assistance for 40,000 families. The remainder of funds would go toward infrastructure projects ($500 million), farmworker housing ($450 million), student housing at the UC and Cal State systems ($350 million), and tribal housing ($200 million).
Additionally, $1.25 billion would be dedicated to home loan assistance for veterans. (This program is not expected to create direct costs as participating veterans would pay monthly payments to the state, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office.)
The need for affordable housing and housing assistance in this state is undeniable. More than two in five households spend, at least, 30% of their incomes on housing.
However, Proposition 1 would only provide a drop in the bucket towards adding to the state’s housing supply, all while hamstringing state spending and burdening taxpayers with decades of debt. The LAO projects that paying off $10 billion in bond debt incurred by this measure would require annual payments between $500 million to $600 million for a quarter of a century. These payments would come from California’s checking account, the General Fund. Because the state has to pay interest on the money it borrows, per the LAO, the total cost of the bond would be about 15% more (after adjusting for inflation) than if the state paid up front with money it already has.
Perhaps that would be acceptable if this burst of spending would make a long-term difference, but it’s doubtful.
Consider that California needs to build 2.5 million new homes, including 1 million affordable ones, to keep up with demand.
But this measure would add only 4% toward the affordable total, and that’s only under pie-in-the-sky circumstances.
More disconcerting is how this measure would do nothing to attack the root of the affordable housing cost problem:
Building subsidized housing in California costs 1.5 times the average cost of building already-exorbitant market-rate housing here, according to a 2025 RAND study.
The nonpartisan think tank identified two major reasons for the discrepancy: Local governments charge “unusually large” architectural and engineering fees, and they require that affordable housing developers pay “substantially above-market” wages.
While $200 million of Proposition 1 would go toward “pilot” programs aimed at developing reduced housing models, at least $10 billion would be spent keeping this bloated model afloat.
Proposition 37
This measure looks great on the surface. It would help Californians buy new homes, all without costing taxpayers a dime.
Well, all that glitters isn’t gold.
Proposition 37 would authorize up to $25 billion in revenue bonds for downpayment assistance on newly constructed homes. Eligible buyers could borrow up to 17% of a home’s purchase price through a fixed-rate second mortgage, making a down payment as low as 3%.
For example, consider an $800,000 home. A buyer could put down $24,000, borrow $136,000 through Proposition 37 and then finance the remaining $640,000 using a conventional mortgage.
A 30-year loan at today’s rates would make the monthly costs of that second mortgage more than $900.
Proposition 37 is not reducing the burden of home prices in California.
It’s not solving the affordability crisis.
It’s just a creative way to help Californians take on more debt.
What rightly worries critics is the terms of these additional loans. When borrowers default, the primary mortgage lender gets repaid first, meaning that the owner of the secondary takes on more risk. That would almost certainly mean that investors would require that buyers pay higher rates on their second mortgages than they pay on the first.
The LAO identifies these financing terms and investor participation as significant uncertainties.
Proposition 37 does nothing to address the main obstacle to homeownership in the state: the monthly cost of a conventional mortgage.
While the majority of renters in the state have incomes that would make them eligible to benefit from the measure’s secondary mortgage program, many wouldn’t qualify for a conventional mortgage in the first place even with its down payment assistance, according to the Public Policy Institute of California.
Far from solving the problem of high home prices, Proposition 37 could compound it.
While the measure restricts using the downpayment assistance to previously unpurchased homes, that does not mean that Proposition 37 will unleash a large new supply of housing.
What’s infinitely more probable is that Proposition 37 would expand purchasing power faster than it would induce new construction — and therefore push up prices.
Homes in California, especially new ones, are sitting unsold longer. In fact, builders have created a glut of new housing in the Central Valley they can’t sell, a dynamic exacerbated as interest rates have climbed. In fact, this summer Fresno topped Realtor.com’s list of U.S. cities with the highest share of new home listings (68%) cutting prices. Photo by Jules Hotz for CalMatters In summary Californians will decide on $44 billion in bonds when the vote on Propositions 1, 37 and 38. They’d take out debt to pay for housing and medical research. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. Your November ballot is welcoming you to make it rain … in bonds. You’ll see an El Nino-sized set of propositions that could flood the housing construction and science research components of the California economy with $44 billion of bond spending if the measures pass. Two of those bond proposals — Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/) for housing and Proposition 38 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) for immunology research — are the traditional borrow-now, pay-back-later arrangements that add a few billion dollars to the overall cost of the propositions. A third, Proposition 37 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/), is an atypical measure that amounts to a low-risk radical experiment that taxpayers likely won’t be on the hook for, at least not directly. Historically, bond propositions win the approval of voters at higher rates than other measures. Since 2000, voters passed 23 of the 26 statewide bonds before them, an 88% yay rate. In recent years voters approved billions in bond debt for school construction, combatting the effects of climate change and housing for veterans. Bonds are a form of debt that the state must pay off over time, and that means annual payments with interest (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/voter-info/overview-state-bond-debt.htm). The state spends $6 billion annually to repay about $80 billion of bonds. Voters and lawmakers have also approved $40 billion in bonds that have yet to be sold. Fortunately for your ballot studying, the following cheat sheet is a primer on just the three bonds before you. Prop. 1: Affordable housing If voters say yes, Prop. 1 would permit California’s treasurer (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/) to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds. That money would provide various types of housing, including to veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes. The measure dedicates $7 billion to constructing, refurbishing, or acquiring apartment complexes, primarily through loans to developers of affordable housing. These developments must serve low-income residents, reserving at least 10% of units for extremely low-income households. Over $1 billion of this total supports permanent and interim housing for the homeless. The bond, if passed, would result in some 40,000 new rental units, wrote (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) the Legislative Analyst’s Office, which is the nonpartisan think-tank of the Legislature. This is the only bond measure on the ballot put forward by lawmakers. The other two secured enough signatures from voters to secure a spot for the November election. Opposition to this bond is minimal. The state Republican Party’s officially neutral on the measure. Several Republican lawmakers in June voted no on the bill that metamorphosed into this bond. They argued that the bill’s title — The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb417) — misled the public on just how much of the bond revenue would support veterans. The answer? $1.25 billion for veterans to secure home loans. Another $350 million would head to the state’s two public university systems to help finance the development of student dorms. But with costs per bed often exceeding $250,000, all those tens of millions of dollars would secure dorms for around 1,300 students. Read CalMatters’ Marisa Kendall’s guide to Prop. 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/). Prop. 37: Help for down payments This bond measure is strange (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-37-homebuyers-loan/), novel and introduces a bevy of unknowns. Confused? So is everyone else, which is why CalMatters’ housing reporter Ben Christopher described this unorthodox proposition as “plainly weird.” (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/) Prop. 37 should be viewed as a way to help buyers of new homes secure down payments. The language permits individuals to apply for as much as 17% of the purchase price of a new house, condo or townhome. That covers much of the typical 20% down payment. Who’s eligible? Roughly 90% of all California renters. The income caps vary by county, so around $115,000 in Imperial and north of $400,000 in San Mateo for a family of three. Eligible homes must satisfy several conditions: They’re new or newly converted and don’t cost more than roughly $1.5 million in the Bay Area or $1 million in Riverside — again, it’s based on a weedy formula by county. What won’t it do? Add to the state’s debt repayment log. This is not a bond that taxpayers will pay back; instead private lenders who provide this bond money will be repaid by homebuyers in the form of interest payments. How many homes this could buy is impossible to predict. That number depends on how much the new homes cost, the incomes of the homebuyers and whether developers build new homes. Most renters today couldn’t afford even the cheapest new homes, said Eric McGhee, an analyst for the nonprofit Public Policy Institute of California who’s written about Prop. 37 (https://www.ppic.org/blog/how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37/). He estimated that anywhere from 60,000 to more than 1.8 million buyers could take advantage of the down payment assistance through this bond measure. The lower end assumes a 20% down payment on the most expensive homes. The higher end assumes 5% down payments on the least expensive homes. Prop. 38: Immunology research This bond proposal (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-38-research-bond/) would commit $4.2 billion to a single, unnamed nonprofit institute that focuses on immunology research and cures for major diseases such as Alzheimer’s, cancer and heart disease. The same amount would be distributed to a committee that’d identify a limited number of researchers at public universities and nonprofits who study immunology and immunotherapies. Previous reporting by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) found only one institute in California currently meets Prop. 38’s criteria for half of the money: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The institute’s primary funder is billionaire Gary K. Michelson, who wrote Prop. 38 and is by far the largest donor to its political campaign. Additional CalMatters reporting raises the question of how ready is the institute to implement the bond’s vast dollars. The institute had only three employees (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) as of last month, far fewer than the 51 it planned to have on staff last year. The Yes on 38 campaign says the bond revenue is needed to hedge against the Trump administration’s ongoing efforts to cut federal science research or limit what’s studied. They argue that any curtailment of drug trials and other therapies can lead to avoidable pain and death for patients of debilitating maladies. Opponents of the measure fault it for concentrating half the money in a single institute and limiting which other researchers can receive the funding. They say science research is best performed in a competitive environment that’s open to all of California’s nonprofit and public university scientists. The problem underlying California’s housing crisis comes down to this: the cost of construction.
It constrains new supply. And the only way to recoup the costs of what does get built requires high rents and mortgages or — in the case of affordable housing — public subsidies.
Unfortunately, the solution to this crisis offered by two statewide propositions has nothing to do with addressing prohibitive building costs. Instead, their answer is to load Californians with debt while delivering bonanzas to home developers and builders.

Endorsement: These three City Council candidates are San Jose’s best choices (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/30/endorsement-elect-peter-ortiz-bien-doan-and-genny-altwer-to-san-jose-city-council/)
Endorsement: Yes on Prop. 3. It asks Californians truly living the California dream to keep paying their fair share. (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/27/endorsement-proposition-3-california-ballot-measure-progressive-income-tax/)
Endorsement: Oakland voters should reject Measure EE plan that politicizes administration (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/23/endorsement-oakland-voters-should-reject-measure-ee-barbara-lee-strong-mayor-sheng-thao/)
Endorsement: Elect Wahab over Hernandez to represent East Bay in Congress (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/22/endorsement-elect-rep-aisha-wahab-melissa-hernandez-cd14-alameda-county-east-bay-swalwell-seat-congress/)
Proposition 1 leaves taxpayers indebted; Proposition 37, homebuyers.
Reject both.
Proposition 1
This measure, placed on the ballot by the state Legislature through Senate Bill 407, is an expensive pandering potpourri of giveaways. Veterans, farmworkers, students, tribes are all the ostensible beneficiaries.
Here’s how it is supposed to work:
Proposition 1 would authorize the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds, all earmarked for various housing programs. The bulk of the bonds, $7.2 billion, would be spent acquiring, building or renovating apartments. The backers of this proposition optimistically estimate that it would subsidize the construction of “up to” 40,000 multifamily rental units as well as 2,500 housing units for farmworkers and 1,200 beds for university students.
Another $1.1 billion would provide homeownership assistance for 40,000 families. The remainder of funds would go toward infrastructure projects ($500 million), farmworker housing ($450 million), student housing at the UC and Cal State systems ($350 million), and tribal housing ($200 million).
Additionally, $1.25 billion would be dedicated to home loan assistance for veterans. (This program is not expected to create direct costs as participating veterans would pay monthly payments to the state, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office.)
The need for affordable housing and housing assistance in this state is undeniable. More than two in five households spend, at least, 30% of their incomes on housing.
However, Proposition 1 would only provide a drop in the bucket towards adding to the state’s housing supply, all while hamstringing state spending and burdening taxpayers with decades of debt. The LAO projects that paying off $10 billion in bond debt incurred by this measure would require annual payments between $500 million to $600 million for a quarter of a century. These payments would come from California’s checking account, the General Fund. Because the state has to pay interest on the money it borrows, per the LAO, the total cost of the bond would be about 15% more (after adjusting for inflation) than if the state paid up front with money it already has.
Perhaps that would be acceptable if this burst of spending would make a long-term difference, but it’s doubtful.
Consider that California needs to build 2.5 million new homes, including 1 million affordable ones, to keep up with demand.
But this measure would add only 4% toward the affordable total, and that’s only under pie-in-the-sky circumstances.
More disconcerting is how this measure would do nothing to attack the root of the affordable housing cost problem:
Building subsidized housing in California costs 1.5 times the average cost of building already-exorbitant market-rate housing here, according to a 2025 RAND study.
The nonpartisan think tank identified two major reasons for the discrepancy: Local governments charge “unusually large” architectural and engineering fees, and they require that affordable housing developers pay “substantially above-market” wages.
While $200 million of Proposition 1 would go toward “pilot” programs aimed at developing reduced housing models, at least $10 billion would be spent keeping this bloated model afloat.
Proposition 37
This measure looks great on the surface. It would help Californians buy new homes, all without costing taxpayers a dime.
Well, all that glitters isn’t gold.
Proposition 37 would authorize up to $25 billion in revenue bonds for downpayment assistance on newly constructed homes. Eligible buyers could borrow up to 17% of a home’s purchase price through a fixed-rate second mortgage, making a down payment as low as 3%.
For example, consider an $800,000 home. A buyer could put down $24,000, borrow $136,000 through Proposition 37 and then finance the remaining $640,000 using a conventional mortgage.
A 30-year loan at today’s rates would make the monthly costs of that second mortgage more than $900.
Proposition 37 is not reducing the burden of home prices in California.
It’s not solving the affordability crisis.
It’s just a creative way to help Californians take on more debt.
What rightly worries critics is the terms of these additional loans. When borrowers default, the primary mortgage lender gets repaid first, meaning that the owner of the secondary takes on more risk. That would almost certainly mean that investors would require that buyers pay higher rates on their second mortgages than they pay on the first.
The LAO identifies these financing terms and investor participation as significant uncertainties.
Proposition 37 does nothing to address the main obstacle to homeownership in the state: the monthly cost of a conventional mortgage.
While the majority of renters in the state have incomes that would make them eligible to benefit from the measure’s secondary mortgage program, many wouldn’t qualify for a conventional mortgage in the first place even with its down payment assistance, according to the Public Policy Institute of California.
Far from solving the problem of high home prices, Proposition 37 could compound it.
While the measure restricts using the downpayment assistance to previously unpurchased homes, that does not mean that Proposition 37 will unleash a large new supply of housing.
What’s infinitely more probable is that Proposition 37 would expand purchasing power faster than it would induce new construction — and therefore push up prices.
Homes in California, especially new ones, are sitting unsold longer. In fact, builders have created a glut of new housing in the Central Valley they can’t sell, a dynamic exacerbated as interest rates have climbed. In fact, this summer Fresno topped Realtor.com’s list of U.S. cities with the highest share of new home listings (68%) cutting prices. Endorsement: Affordable housing in California isn’t going to pay for itself. Is Prop 1 the answer?
Proposition 1 would authorize California to issue $11.25 billion in new bonds to create and preserve affordable housing and expand opportunities for owning a home.
S.F. Chronicle illustration from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 26, 2026
The housing debate in California often feels a bit like fighting with your rambling uncle during Thanksgiving dinner. But there’s generally one island of universal agreement in a sea of rage: the need for more affordable housing.
A recent legislative analysis found (https://ahcd.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2026-04/ahcd-hearing-packet-for-the-website.pdf) that 2.2 million extremely low-income and low-income California households are competing for just 664,000 affordable rental homes. To even come close to meeting demand, the California Department of Housing and Community Development estimated the state needs at least 1 million new affordable units by 2031, (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/sites/default/files/docs/policy-and-research/plan-report/StateofCADraft-2022-2023-AAP-12-6-22.pdf) including about 47,000 in San Francisco (https://sfgov.legistar.com/View.ashx?GUID=EDE50759-96D2-4873-846C-70851EEE4957&ID=15560084&M=F&).
Building this level of subsidized affordable housing will be neither easy nor cheap — and there’s lots of competition for limited funds.
In 2018, voters approved $4 billion in bonds for affordable and veteran housing (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=1&year=2018), all of which was allocated by the end of 2023. California’s Multifamily Housing Program (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/funding/mhp) — the state’s primary vehicle for providing developers with low-cost loans to build, rehabilitate and preserve affordable housing — has $9 in requests for every dollar available, a California Budget and Policy Center analysis found (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/proposition-1-californias-veterans-and-affordable-housing-bond/).

Endorsement : Who should replace Nancy Pelosi in Congress? It’s not even a choice (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/scott-wiener-connie-chan-pelosi-22448323.php)
Proposition 1 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop1-text-proposed-laws.pdf), which the state Legislature placed on the November ballot with bipartisan support (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417), would authorize California to issue $11.25 billion in new bonds to create and preserve affordable housing and expand homeownership opportunities. Befitting the broad consensus on the state’s affordability crisis, it has no formal opposition.
The measure is rigidly prescriptive in its allocation of funds.
It allocates $7.2 billion to the Multifamily Housing Program — which the measure’s author, Assembly Member Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland, described in an endorsement interview as the “workhorse” of California’s efforts to develop affordable rental homes. Of that pool, $1.15 billion would be reserved for supportive housing and services for people at risk of or exiting homelessness, with $150 million set aside for youth who are homeless or in foster care. Another $750 million would go to renovating and modernizing existing affordable housing.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Outside of that bucket, $1.25 billion is earmarked for the CalVet Home Loan program (https://www.calvet.ca.gov/HomeLoans), which uses the proceeds from bond sales to provide loans to veterans to purchase homes. This program doesn’t cost taxpayers anything because veterans repay the cost of the bonds and interest through their loan payments. (Some Republican lawmakers accused Democrats of trying to inflate voter support for the measure by calling it the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond when only about 10% of the overall funds go to veterans.)
Another $600 million would go to local agencies and nonprofits — such as Habitat for Humanity — to work with would-be homeowners to build or finance affordable homes, while $500 million would go to down-payment assistance for eligible first-time home buyers.
Among the measure’s other earmarks: $500 million for developing infrastructure — such as water and sewage lines — to support affordable housing, $450 million to build and rehabilitate farmworker housing, $350 million to be split evenly between the University of California and California State University systems for student housing, $200 million to tribal housing programs and $200 million to local grants and pilot programs that “demonstrate innovative, cost-saving approaches to creating or preserving affordable housing.”
If this seems like a dizzying array of priorities, that’s because it is.

Your endorsement of Scott Wiener deserves a closer examination of the philosophy behind his housing and wealth policies.
Unequal wealth is a fact; it does not, by itself, establish an injustice or a government duty to reduce it. People build wealth through work, saving, investment, entrepreneurship, risk and circumstance. Wiener’s policies reflect a different premise: that disparities in wealth and access to affluent communities are problems government should correct through taxation and housing policy. His housing policies use state authority to require communities—including affluent, low-density communities—to accommodate housing across income levels, with consequences for noncompliance. This shifts important land-use decisions from local communities to the state.Meanwhile, many Californians earn too much for substantial assistance but too little to buy homes in expensive communities. Policy should focus on upward mobility—better schools, safer communities, etc. - not simply equal $$
Prop 1 is the product of years of legislative sausage-making: It combines bits and pieces of policies proposed by lawmakers and advocates, each with a specific group or issue they’re trying to address.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
So, is the measure too unwieldy — and divided among too many different groups and interests — to be effective?
Wicks told us she is “very aware of that concern” but emphasized that each of the programs receiving funding in the bond is “a proven model that we know works.”
Altogether, Prop 1 could subsidize the creation of as many as 40,000 affordable rental units, plus 2,500 for farmworkers and another 1,200 for college students, according to estimates from the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) — while helping 40,000 households, including 2,100 veterans, achieve homeownership. (A separate November ballot measure, Prop 37 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-37-housing-home-loans-22422795.php), would provide down-payment assistance to middle-income Californians, at no cost to taxpayers.)
This, of course, is a drop in the bucket of California’s housing needs — at a not insignificant cost. The state will need to make estimated annual payments of $500 million to $600 million from the general fund for 25 years to pay off the bond — 15% more expensive than an upfront payment. This will also reduce the money available for other critical programs at a time when California faces years of projected future budget deficits (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5101).
But there is good reason to believe that California will, as Wicks put it, “have a better ROI on these resources today” than in the past.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
That’s because the state has in recent years significantly reduced the roadblocks that delay housing and drive up the cost of production — including by exempting all infill development from unnecessary review (https://www.sfchronicle.com/california/article/ceqa-housing-roadblocks-newsom-20402835.php) under the California Environmental Quality Act and streamlining dense housing near transit (https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/housing-transit-map-yimby-21075831.php).
Ongoing efforts to streamline the state’s maze of affordable housing financing programs (https://lao.ca.gov/publications/report/5199) into one consolidated application (https://ahcd.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2026-08/ab-519-july-2026-deliverable-7.1.26-final-afforable-housing-finance-workgroup.pdf), along with other reforms, could also slash development costs by $60,000 to $70,000 per unit (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/about-hcd/newsroom/more-housing-faster-governor-newsom-signs-historic-housing-affordability-reforms).
“We’re at a great moment in time to actually have the best impact on housing that I’ve seen in my career,” Ray Pearl, executive director of the California Housing Consortium, told us.
One thing the measure doesn’t fully account for: upkeep. As the Chronicle has rigorously documented (https://www.sfchronicle.com/projects/2022/san-francisco-sros/), many deed-restricted affordable homes in places like San Francisco are deteriorating. (https://www.sfchronicle.com/sf/article/affordable-housing-sale-21251741.php) Prop 1 only sets aside a relative pittance for rehabilitation.
This is a fundamental problem with California’s focus on 100% affordable housing developments — rents don’t cover the bills, necessitating significant ongoing subsidies.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Legislators would be wise to pursue other paths, such as Washington state’s tax incentives (https://www.theurbanist.org/state-senate-greenlights-sweeping-tod-housing-bill/) to build affordable units inside market-rate developments, to share the burden of upkeep with the private sector.
Wicks told us California also needs to restructure its budgets to establish “sustained ongoing funding for affordable housing so that we’re not having to have this bond conversation every six years.”
About Opinion

Its judgments are made independent of the news operation , which covers the news without consideration of our editorial positions.
We agree.
In the interim, however, the need for more affordable housing is too desperate to wait. Prop 1 is well-positioned to reap the benefits of the state’s new streamlining laws. We recommend a yes vote.

Read McClatchy Media’s endorsement on California’s Proposition 1 | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Updated September 30, 2026 2:22 PM
A drone view of Mirasol Village on Monday, Aug. 3, 2026. Proposition 1 looks to increase homebuilding in California through an $11.25 billion bond measure.
HECTOR AMEZCUA
hamezcua@sacbee.com
California has spent years creating laws that make it easier to build housing. Now it needs to help finance affordable housing (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=1&year=2026&utm_source=chatgpt.com) waiting to be produced at rents many Californians can afford.
There are nearly 40,000 affordable rental homes in the development pipeline (https://www.housingfinance.com/data-trends/california-pipeline-holds-nearly-40000-affordable-homes-seeking-funds) — designed and approved but awaiting sufficient financing to begin construction, according to Enterprise Community Partners, (https://www.enterprisecommunity.org/about) a national housing nonprofit. Proposition 1 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317117857.html) could help close those financing gaps.
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 1 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317117857.html)
A “yes” vote on Proposition 1 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_1,_Veteran_and_Housing_Assistance_Programs_Bond_Measure_(2026)) would authorize $11.25 billion in bonds: $10 billion for affordable housing and $1.25 billion for a longstandingCalVet home-loan program. (https://veteran.com/start/?src=adw&adg=185122315662&cmp=compterms&desc=calculator&matchtype=p&adid=803809597618&targetid=kwd-297340664879&label=&campaignid=23211217847&extid=&gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=23211217847&gbraid=0AAAAAqq9dHmkha--aWxuqkJFb13gc3lv2&gclid=CjwKCAjwq8PVBhAKEiwA2i3SHZePD1ETl_2tqMBf65xQCzjoSQ7GCNQ3Jj7lr4UZqy9t2I0slreQtBoCALsQAvD_BwE) Funds raised by Prop. 1 would support construction and preservation of affordable apartments (https://www.enterprisecommunity.org/learning-center/resources/2026-california-affordable-housing-production-pipeline?utm_source=chatgpt.com), supportive housing, homeownership assistance, farmworker and tribal housing, student housing and infrastructure needed for affordable developments.
It’s undeniable that Californians struggle with rents they cannot afford, homelessness and home prices that put ownership beyond the reach of many working families.
Private developers generally cannot build housing for low-income and extremely low-income households and charge rents these families can afford while recovering the cost of construction. Every dollar the state invests leverages $4 from federal, local and private funding, according to the California Budget & Policy Center.
And taxpayers wouldn’t be purchasing a fleeting benefit. Affordable apartments receiving these subsidies generally must remain affordable for 55 years. Proponents estimate that turnover during that period could allow roughly 500,000 households to benefit.
There is a cost. TheLegislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/) estimates that repaying the $10 billion housing bond will cost the state’s General Fund $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years — roughly one-quarter of 1% of today’s General Fund budget. The separate $1.25 billion veterans portion is expected to be repaid through veterans’ mortgage payments, as previous CalVet bonds have been.
Opponents rightly say that housing in California is too expensive to build. But their argument that lawmakers should attack those costs instead of subsidizing affordable housing presents a false choice.
California can do both.
In just the past two legislative sessions, for instance, lawmakers have approved a series of changes to speed up environmental reviews and permitting, reduce some impact fees and simplify affordable-housing financing. The state’s newOne-Stop Shop financing reforms (https://ternercenter.berkeley.edu/research-and-policy/california-governors-budget-proposal-advances-a-one-stop-shop-for-affordable-housing/) and impact-fee changes alone are estimated by the Newsom administration to reduce affordable housing costs by $60,000-$70,000 per unit.
Government should eliminate unnecessary expenses, but it cannot eliminate the real costs of roads, schools, water, sewer and other infrastructure communities need as they grow. Nor is government responsible for every rising construction expense. Land, materials, interest rates, insurance, labor, contractor practices and other factors all contribute.
That’s why Proposition 1 should become something more than another infusion of money. California should use this enormous investment to learn precisely why affordable housing costs what it does.
For every project receiving bond money, the state should collect standardized information about land, construction, financing, permit and impact fees, professional services, labor expense, financing sources, approval times and change orders. This would allow researchers to compare similar projects being financed and determine why one costs $450,000 per unit while another costs $800,000 a unit.
And Californians should not have to become government accounting detectives to find the results.
The state should create a simple, prominently displayed public dashboard showing money awarded and spent, units produced and preserved, project locations, costs per unit and completion times. Proponents agreed with us that such transparency is achievable.
That need became obvious when we asked them what measurable results from California’s 2018 housing bond justify returning to voters for substantially more money. They cited strong demand and the fact that its funding was fully committed within five years, but could not readily provide the kind of statewide performance measures voters deserve.
Housing is fundamental to economic mobility. A family struggling to keep a roof over its head has little opportunity to save, educate its children, emphasize wellness or build financial security.
California needs those homes. It also needs to learn how to build the next ones faster and for less.
Proposition 1 gives California (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/proposition-1-californias-veterans-and-affordable-housing-bond/) the opportunity to do better.

Endorsement: Affordable housing in California isn’t going to pay for itself. Is Prop 1 the answer?
Proposition 1 would authorize California to issue $11.25 billion in new bonds to create and preserve affordable housing and expand opportunities for owning a home.
S.F. Chronicle illustration from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 26, 2026
The housing debate in California often feels a bit like fighting with your rambling uncle during Thanksgiving dinner. But there’s generally one island of universal agreement in a sea of rage: the need for more affordable housing.
A recent legislative analysis found (https://ahcd.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2026-04/ahcd-hearing-packet-for-the-website.pdf) that 2.2 million extremely low-income and low-income California households are competing for just 664,000 affordable rental homes. Read McClatchy Media’s endorsement on California’s Proposition 1 | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Updated September 30, 2026 2:22 PM
A drone view of Mirasol Village on Monday, Aug. 3, 2026. Proposition 1 looks to increase homebuilding in California through an $11.25 billion bond measure.
HECTOR AMEZCUA
hamezcua@sacbee.com
California has spent years creating laws that make it easier to build housing. Now it needs to help finance affordable housing (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=1&year=2026&utm_source=chatgpt.com) waiting to be produced at rents many Californians can afford.
There are nearly 40,000 affordable rental homes in the development pipeline (https://www.housingfinance.com/data-trends/california-pipeline-holds-nearly-40000-affordable-homes-seeking-funds) — designed and approved but awaiting sufficient financing to begin construction, according to Enterprise Community Partners, (https://www.enterprisecommunity.org/about) a national housing nonprofit. Proposition 1 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317117857.html) could help close those financing gaps.
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 1 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317117857.html)
A “yes” vote on Proposition 1 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_1,_Veteran_and_Housing_Assistance_Programs_Bond_Measure_(2026)) would authorize $11.25 billion in bonds: $10 billion for affordable housing and $1.25 billion for a longstandingCalVet home-loan program. (https://veteran.com/start/?src=adw&adg=185122315662&cmp=compterms&desc=calculator&matchtype=p&adid=803809597618&targetid=kwd-297340664879&label=&campaignid=23211217847&extid=&gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=23211217847&gbraid=0AAAAAqq9dHmkha--aWxuqkJFb13gc3lv2&gclid=CjwKCAjwq8PVBhAKEiwA2i3SHZePD1ETl_2tqMBf65xQCzjoSQ7GCNQ3Jj7lr4UZqy9t2I0slreQtBoCALsQAvD_BwE) Funds raised by Prop. 1 would support construction and preservation of affordable apartments (https://www.enterprisecommunity.org/learning-center/resources/2026-california-affordable-housing-production-pipeline?utm_source=chatgpt.com), supportive housing, homeownership assistance, farmworker and tribal housing, student housing and infrastructure needed for affordable developments.
It’s undeniable that Californians struggle with rents they cannot afford, homelessness and home prices that put ownership beyond the reach of many working families.
Private developers generally cannot build housing for low-income and extremely low-income households and charge rents these families can afford while recovering the cost of construction. Every dollar the state invests leverages $4 from federal, local and private funding, according to the California Budget & Policy Center.
And taxpayers wouldn’t be purchasing a fleeting benefit. Affordable apartments receiving these subsidies generally must remain affordable for 55 years. Proponents estimate that turnover during that period could allow roughly 500,000 households to benefit.
There is a cost. TheLegislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/) estimates that repaying the $10 billion housing bond will cost the state’s General Fund $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years — roughly one-quarter of 1% of today’s General Fund budget. The separate $1.25 billion veterans portion is expected to be repaid through veterans’ mortgage payments, as previous CalVet bonds have been.
Opponents rightly say that housing in California is too expensive to build. But their argument that lawmakers should attack those costs instead of subsidizing affordable housing presents a false choice.
California can do both.
In just the past two legislative sessions, for instance, lawmakers have approved a series of changes to speed up environmental reviews and permitting, reduce some impact fees and simplify affordable-housing financing. The state’s newOne-Stop Shop financing reforms (https://ternercenter.berkeley.edu/research-and-policy/california-governors-budget-proposal-advances-a-one-stop-shop-for-affordable-housing/) and impact-fee changes alone are estimated by the Newsom administration to reduce affordable housing costs by $60,000-$70,000 per unit.
Government should eliminate unnecessary expenses, but it cannot eliminate the real costs of roads, schools, water, sewer and other infrastructure communities need as they grow. Nor is government responsible for every rising construction expense. Land, materials, interest rates, insurance, labor, contractor practices and other factors all contribute.
That’s why Proposition 1 should become something more than another infusion of money. California should use this enormous investment to learn precisely why affordable housing costs what it does.
For every project receiving bond money, the state should collect standardized information about land, construction, financing, permit and impact fees, professional services, labor expense, financing sources, approval times and change orders. This would allow researchers to compare similar projects being financed and determine why one costs $450,000 per unit while another costs $800,000 a unit.
And Californians should not have to become government accounting detectives to find the results.
The state should create a simple, prominently displayed public dashboard showing money awarded and spent, units produced and preserved, project locations, costs per unit and completion times. Proponents agreed with us that such transparency is achievable.
That need became obvious when we asked them what measurable results from California’s 2018 housing bond justify returning to voters for substantially more money. They cited strong demand and the fact that its funding was fully committed within five years, but could not readily provide the kind of statewide performance measures voters deserve.
Housing is fundamental to economic mobility. A family struggling to keep a roof over its head has little opportunity to save, educate its children, emphasize wellness or build financial security.
California needs those homes. It also needs to learn how to build the next ones faster and for less.
Proposition 1 gives California (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/proposition-1-californias-veterans-and-affordable-housing-bond/) the opportunity to do better.
