The bill to put this item on the ballot also was widely supported by organizations that provide low-income housing, plus various municipal governments, including San Diego, Orange and Santa Barbara counties.
Who are the opponents?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Republicans, who represented all of the votes against Proposition 1, said on the legislative floor that the state instead should curtail building regulations to bring down the cost of housing without burdening taxpayers.
“We know the cost of building in California is extraordinarily, exponentially higher than it needs to be,” said Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, a Republican who represents cities and towns just east of San Diego. “We need reforms first before we take out the credit card and borrow money.”

Here’s what $44 billion would buy by Mikhail Zinshteyn (https://calmatters.org/author/mikhailzinshteyn/) October 24, 2026 Updated October 25, 2026 Republish Share this: Share on X (Opens in new window) X (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/bond-measures-on-california-ballot/) Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/bond-measures-on-california-ballot/) Share on WhatsApp (Opens in new window) WhatsApp (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/bond-measures-on-california-ballot/) Construction in a residential area that was burned during the Eaton Fire in 2025, in Altadena, on Aug. 3, 2026. Photo by Jules Hotz for CalMatters In summary Californians will decide on $44 billion in bonds when the vote on Propositions 1, 37 and 38. They’d take out debt to pay for housing and medical research. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. Your November ballot is welcoming you to make it rain … in bonds. You’ll see an El Nino-sized set of propositions that could flood the housing construction and science research components of the California economy with $44 billion of bond spending if the measures pass. Two of those bond proposals — Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/) for housing and Proposition 38 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) for immunology research — are the traditional borrow-now, pay-back-later arrangements that add a few billion dollars to the overall cost of the propositions. A third, Proposition 37 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/), is an atypical measure that amounts to a low-risk radical experiment that taxpayers likely won’t be on the hook for, at least not directly. Historically, bond propositions win the approval of voters at higher rates than other measures. Since 2000, voters passed 23 of the 26 statewide bonds before them, an 88% yay rate. In recent years voters approved billions in bond debt for school construction, combatting the effects of climate change and housing for veterans. Bonds are a form of debt that the state must pay off over time, and that means annual payments with interest (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/voter-info/overview-state-bond-debt.htm). The state spends $6 billion annually to repay about $80 billion of bonds. Voters and lawmakers have also approved $40 billion in bonds that have yet to be sold. Fortunately for your ballot studying, the following cheat sheet is a primer on just the three bonds before you. Prop. 1: Affordable housing If voters say yes, Prop. 1 would permit California’s treasurer (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/) to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds. That money would provide various types of housing, including to veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes. The measure dedicates $7 billion to constructing, refurbishing, or acquiring apartment complexes, primarily through loans to developers of affordable housing. These developments must serve low-income residents, reserving at least 10% of units for extremely low-income households. Over $1 billion of this total supports permanent and interim housing for the homeless. The bond, if passed, would result in some 40,000 new rental units, wrote (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) the Legislative Analyst’s Office, which is the nonpartisan think-tank of the Legislature. This is the only bond measure on the ballot put forward by lawmakers. The other two secured enough signatures from voters to secure a spot for the November election. Opposition to this bond is minimal. The state Republican Party’s officially neutral on the measure. Several Republican lawmakers in June voted no on the bill that metamorphosed into this bond. They argued that the bill’s title — The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb417) — misled the public on just how much of the bond revenue would support veterans. The answer? $1.25 billion for veterans to secure home loans. Another $350 million would head to the state’s two public university systems to help finance the development of student dorms. But with costs per bed often exceeding $250,000, all those tens of millions of dollars would secure dorms for around 1,300 students. Get California’s most essential headlines without feeling overwhelmed. Email address By clicking subscribe, you agree to the terms (https://calmatters.org/about/policies-and-standards/). Sign up for free Δ Support for Prop. 1 is vast, including Gov. Gavin Newsom, the state Democratic party, home-sharing company AirBnB, major unions and more. Want more? Read CalMatters’ Marisa Kendall’s guide to Prop. 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/). Prop. 37: Help for down payments This bond measure is strange (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-37-homebuyers-loan/), novel and introduces a bevy of unknowns. Confused? So is everyone else, which is why CalMatters’ housing reporter Ben Christopher described this unorthodox proposition as “plainly weird.” (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/) Prop. 37 should be viewed as a way to help buyers of new homes secure down payments. The language permits individuals to apply for as much as 17% of the purchase price of a new house, condo or townhome. That covers much of the typical 20% down payment. Who’s eligible? Roughly 90% of all California renters. The income caps vary by county, so around $115,000 in Imperial and north of $400,000 in San Mateo for a family of three. Eligible homes must satisfy several conditions: They’re new or newly converted and don’t cost more than roughly $1.5 million in the Bay Area or $1 million in Riverside — again, it’s based on a weedy formula by county. What won’t it do? Add to the state’s debt repayment log. This is not a bond that taxpayers will pay back; instead private lenders who provide this bond money will be repaid by homebuyers in the form of interest payments. How many homes this could buy is impossible to predict. That number depends on how much the new homes cost, the incomes of the homebuyers and whether developers build new homes. Most renters today couldn’t afford even the cheapest new homes, said Eric McGhee, an analyst for the nonprofit Public Policy Institute of California who’s written about Prop. 37 (https://www.ppic.org/blog/how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37/). He estimated that anywhere from 60,000 to more than 1.8 million buyers could take advantage of the down payment assistance through this bond measure. The lower end assumes a 20% down payment on the most expensive homes. The higher end assumes 5% down payments on the least expensive homes. Prop. 38: Immunology research This bond proposal (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-38-research-bond/) would commit $4.2 billion to a single, unnamed nonprofit institute that focuses on immunology research and cures for major diseases such as Alzheimer’s, cancer and heart disease. The same amount would be distributed to a committee that’d identify a limited number of researchers at public universities and nonprofits who study immunology and immunotherapies. Previous reporting by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) found only one institute in California currently meets Prop. 38’s criteria for half of the money: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The institute’s primary funder is billionaire Gary K. Michelson, who wrote Prop. 38 and is by far the largest donor to its political campaign. Additional CalMatters reporting raises the question of how ready is the institute to implement the bond’s vast dollars. The institute had only three employees (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) as of last month, far fewer than the 51 it planned to have on staff last year. The Yes on 38 campaign says the bond revenue is needed to hedge against the Trump administration’s ongoing efforts to cut federal science research or limit what’s studied. They argue that any curtailment of drug trials and other therapies can lead to avoidable pain and death for patients of debilitating maladies. Opponents of the measure fault it for concentrating half the money in a single institute and limiting which other researchers can receive the funding. They say science research is best performed in a competitive environment that’s open to all of California’s nonprofit and public university scientists. The problem underlying California’s housing crisis comes down to this: the cost of construction.
It constrains new supply. And the only way to recoup the costs of what does get built requires high rents and mortgages or — in the case of affordable housing — public subsidies.
Unfortunately, the solution to this crisis offered by two statewide propositions has nothing to do with addressing prohibitive building costs. Instead, their answer is to load Californians with debt while delivering bonanzas to home developers and builders.

Proposition 1 leaves taxpayers indebted; Proposition 37, homebuyers.
Reject both.
Proposition 1
This measure, placed on the ballot by the state Legislature through Senate Bill 407, is an expensive pandering potpourri of giveaways. Veterans, farmworkers, students, tribes are all the ostensible beneficiaries.
Here’s how it is supposed to work:
Proposition 1 would authorize the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds, all earmarked for various housing programs. The bulk of the bonds, $7.2 billion, would be spent acquiring, building or renovating apartments. The backers of this proposition optimistically estimate that it would subsidize the construction of “up to” 40,000 multifamily rental units as well as 2,500 housing units for farmworkers and 1,200 beds for university students.
Another $1.1 billion would provide homeownership assistance for 40,000 families. The remainder of funds would go toward infrastructure projects ($500 million), farmworker housing ($450 million), student housing at the UC and Cal State systems ($350 million), and tribal housing ($200 million).
Additionally, $1.25 billion would be dedicated to home loan assistance for veterans. (This program is not expected to create direct costs as participating veterans would pay monthly payments to the state, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office.)
The need for affordable housing and housing assistance in this state is undeniable. More than two in five households spend, at least, 30% of their incomes on housing.
However, Proposition 1 would only provide a drop in the bucket towards adding to the state’s housing supply, all while hamstringing state spending and burdening taxpayers with decades of debt. The LAO projects that paying off $10 billion in bond debt incurred by this measure would require annual payments between $500 million to $600 million for a quarter of a century. These payments would come from California’s checking account, the General Fund. Because the state has to pay interest on the money it borrows, per the LAO, the total cost of the bond would be about 15% more (after adjusting for inflation) than if the state paid up front with money it already has.
Perhaps that would be acceptable if this burst of spending would make a long-term difference, but it’s doubtful.
Consider that California needs to build 2.5 million new homes, including 1 million affordable ones, to keep up with demand.
But this measure would add only 4% toward the affordable total, and that’s only under pie-in-the-sky circumstances.
More disconcerting is how this measure would do nothing to attack the root of the affordable housing cost problem:
Building subsidized housing in California costs 1.5 times the average cost of building already-exorbitant market-rate housing here, according to a 2025 RAND study.
The nonpartisan think tank identified two major reasons for the discrepancy: Local governments charge “unusually large” architectural and engineering fees, and they require that affordable housing developers pay “substantially above-market” wages.
While $200 million of Proposition 1 would go toward “pilot” programs aimed at developing reduced housing models, at least $10 billion would be spent keeping this bloated model afloat.
Proposition 37
This measure looks great on the surface. It would help Californians buy new homes, all without costing taxpayers a dime.
Well, all that glitters isn’t gold.
Proposition 37 would authorize up to $25 billion in revenue bonds for downpayment assistance on newly constructed homes. Eligible buyers could borrow up to 17% of a home’s purchase price through a fixed-rate second mortgage, making a down payment as low as 3%.
For example, consider an $800,000 home. A buyer could put down $24,000, borrow $136,000 through Proposition 37 and then finance the remaining $640,000 using a conventional mortgage.
A 30-year loan at today’s rates would make the monthly costs of that second mortgage more than $900.
Proposition 37 is not reducing the burden of home prices in California.
It’s not solving the affordability crisis.
It’s just a creative way to help Californians take on more debt.
What rightly worries critics is the terms of these additional loans. When borrowers default, the primary mortgage lender gets repaid first, meaning that the owner of the secondary takes on more risk. That would almost certainly mean that investors would require that buyers pay higher rates on their second mortgages than they pay on the first.
The LAO identifies these financing terms and investor participation as significant uncertainties.
Proposition 37 does nothing to address the main obstacle to homeownership in the state: the monthly cost of a conventional mortgage.
While the majority of renters in the state have incomes that would make them eligible to benefit from the measure’s secondary mortgage program, many wouldn’t qualify for a conventional mortgage in the first place even with its down payment assistance, according to the Public Policy Institute of California.
Far from solving the problem of high home prices, Proposition 37 could compound it.
While the measure restricts using the downpayment assistance to previously unpurchased homes, that does not mean that Proposition 37 will unleash a large new supply of housing.
What’s infinitely more probable is that Proposition 37 would expand purchasing power faster than it would induce new construction — and therefore push up prices.
Homes in California, especially new ones, are sitting unsold longer. In fact, builders have created a glut of new housing in the Central Valley they can’t sell, a dynamic exacerbated as interest rates have climbed. Endorsement: Affordable housing in California isn’t going to pay for itself. Is Prop 1 the answer?
Proposition 1 would authorize California to issue $11.25 billion in new bonds to create and preserve affordable housing and expand opportunities for owning a home.
S.F. Chronicle illustration from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 26, 2026
The housing debate in California often feels a bit like fighting with your rambling uncle during Thanksgiving dinner. But there’s generally one island of universal agreement in a sea of rage: the need for more affordable housing.
A recent legislative analysis found (https://ahcd.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2026-04/ahcd-hearing-packet-for-the-website.pdf) that 2.2 million extremely low-income and low-income California households are competing for just 664,000 affordable rental homes. To even come close to meeting demand, the California Department of Housing and Community Development estimated the state needs at least 1 million new affordable units by 2031, (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/sites/default/files/docs/policy-and-research/plan-report/StateofCADraft-2022-2023-AAP-12-6-22.pdf) including about 47,000 in San Francisco (https://sfgov.legistar.com/View.ashx?GUID=EDE50759-96D2-4873-846C-70851EEE4957&ID=15560084&M=F&).
Building this level of subsidized affordable housing will be neither easy nor cheap — and there’s lots of competition for limited funds.
In 2018, voters approved $4 billion in bonds for affordable and veteran housing (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=1&year=2018), all of which was allocated by the end of 2023. California’s Multifamily Housing Program (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/funding/mhp) — the state’s primary vehicle for providing developers with low-cost loans to build, rehabilitate and preserve affordable housing — has $9 in requests for every dollar available, a California Budget and Policy Center analysis found (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/proposition-1-californias-veterans-and-affordable-housing-bond/).

Proposition 1 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop1-text-proposed-laws.pdf), which the state Legislature placed on the November ballot with bipartisan support (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417), would authorize California to issue $11.25 billion in new bonds to create and preserve affordable housing and expand homeownership opportunities. Befitting the broad consensus on the state’s affordability crisis, it has no formal opposition.
The measure is rigidly prescriptive in its allocation of funds.
It allocates $7.2 billion to the Multifamily Housing Program — which the measure’s author, Assembly Member Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland, described in an endorsement interview as the “workhorse” of California’s efforts to develop affordable rental homes. Of that pool, $1.15 billion would be reserved for supportive housing and services for people at risk of or exiting homelessness, with $150 million set aside for youth who are homeless or in foster care. Another $750 million would go to renovating and modernizing existing affordable housing.

Article continues below this ad
Outside of that bucket, $1.25 billion is earmarked for the CalVet Home Loan program (https://www.calvet.ca.gov/HomeLoans), which uses the proceeds from bond sales to provide loans to veterans to purchase homes. This program doesn’t cost taxpayers anything because veterans repay the cost of the bonds and interest through their loan payments. (Some Republican lawmakers accused Democrats of trying to inflate voter support for the measure by calling it the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond when only about 10% of the overall funds go to veterans.)
Another $600 million would go to local agencies and nonprofits — such as Habitat for Humanity — to work with would-be homeowners to build or finance affordable homes, while $500 million would go to down-payment assistance for eligible first-time home buyers.
Among the measure’s other earmarks: $500 million for developing infrastructure — such as water and sewage lines — to support affordable housing, $450 million to build and rehabilitate farmworker housing, $350 million to be split evenly between the University of California and California State University systems for student housing, $200 million to tribal housing programs and $200 million to local grants and pilot programs that “demonstrate innovative, cost-saving approaches to creating or preserving affordable housing.”
If this seems like a dizzying array of priorities, that’s because it is.

Your endorsement of Scott Wiener deserves a closer examination of the philosophy behind his housing and wealth policies.
Unequal wealth is a fact; it does not, by itself, establish an injustice or a government duty to reduce it. People build wealth through work, saving, investment, entrepreneurship, risk and circumstance. Wiener’s policies reflect a different premise: that disparities in wealth and access to affluent communities are problems government should correct through taxation and housing policy. His housing policies use state authority to require communities—including affluent, low-density communities—to accommodate housing across income levels, with consequences for noncompliance. This shifts important land-use decisions from local communities to the state.Meanwhile, many Californians earn too much for substantial assistance but too little to buy homes in expensive communities. Policy should focus on upward mobility—better schools, safer communities, etc. - not simply equal $$
Prop 1 is the product of years of legislative sausage-making: It combines bits and pieces of policies proposed by lawmakers and advocates, each with a specific group or issue they’re trying to address.

So, is the measure too unwieldy — and divided among too many different groups and interests — to be effective?
Wicks told us she is “very aware of that concern” but emphasized that each of the programs receiving funding in the bond is “a proven model that we know works.”
Altogether, Prop 1 could subsidize the creation of as many as 40,000 affordable rental units, plus 2,500 for farmworkers and another 1,200 for college students, according to estimates from the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) — while helping 40,000 households, including 2,100 veterans, achieve homeownership. (A separate November ballot measure, Prop 37 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-37-housing-home-loans-22422795.php), would provide down-payment assistance to middle-income Californians, at no cost to taxpayers.)
This, of course, is a drop in the bucket of California’s housing needs — at a not insignificant cost. The state will need to make estimated annual payments of $500 million to $600 million from the general fund for 25 years to pay off the bond — 15% more expensive than an upfront payment. This will also reduce the money available for other critical programs at a time when California faces years of projected future budget deficits (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5101).
But there is good reason to believe that California will, as Wicks put it, “have a better ROI on these resources today” than in the past.

That’s because the state has in recent years significantly reduced the roadblocks that delay housing and drive up the cost of production — including by exempting all infill development from unnecessary review (https://www.sfchronicle.com/california/article/ceqa-housing-roadblocks-newsom-20402835.php) under the California Environmental Quality Act and streamlining dense housing near transit (https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/housing-transit-map-yimby-21075831.php).
Ongoing efforts to streamline the state’s maze of affordable housing financing programs (https://lao.ca.gov/publications/report/5199) into one consolidated application (https://ahcd.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2026-08/ab-519-july-2026-deliverable-7.1.26-final-afforable-housing-finance-workgroup.pdf), along with other reforms, could also slash development costs by $60,000 to $70,000 per unit (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/about-hcd/newsroom/more-housing-faster-governor-newsom-signs-historic-housing-affordability-reforms).
“We’re at a great moment in time to actually have the best impact on housing that I’ve seen in my career,” Ray Pearl, executive director of the California Housing Consortium, told us.
One thing the measure doesn’t fully account for: upkeep. As the Chronicle has rigorously documented (https://www.sfchronicle.com/projects/2022/san-francisco-sros/), many deed-restricted affordable homes in places like San Francisco are deteriorating. (https://www.sfchronicle.com/sf/article/affordable-housing-sale-21251741.php) Prop 1 only sets aside a relative pittance for rehabilitation.
This is a fundamental problem with California’s focus on 100% affordable housing developments — rents don’t cover the bills, necessitating significant ongoing subsidies.

Legislators would be wise to pursue other paths, such as Washington state’s tax incentives (https://www.theurbanist.org/state-senate-greenlights-sweeping-tod-housing-bill/) to build affordable units inside market-rate developments, to share the burden of upkeep with the private sector.
Wicks told us California also needs to restructure its budgets to establish “sustained ongoing funding for affordable housing so that we’re not having to have this bond conversation every six years.”

By McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Updated September 30, 2026 2:22 PM
A drone view of Mirasol Village on Monday, Aug. 3, 2026. Proposition 1 looks to increase homebuilding in California through an $11.25 billion bond measure.
HECTOR AMEZCUA
hamezcua@sacbee.com
California has spent years creating laws that make it easier to build housing. Now it needs to help finance affordable housing (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=1&year=2026&utm_source=chatgpt.com) waiting to be produced at rents many Californians can afford.
There are nearly 40,000 affordable rental homes in the development pipeline (https://www.housingfinance.com/data-trends/california-pipeline-holds-nearly-40000-affordable-homes-seeking-funds) — designed and approved but awaiting sufficient financing to begin construction, according to Enterprise Community Partners, (https://www.enterprisecommunity.org/about) a national housing nonprofit. Proposition 1 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317117857.html) could help close those financing gaps.
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 1 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317117857.html)
A “yes” vote on Proposition 1 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_1,_Veteran_and_Housing_Assistance_Programs_Bond_Measure_(2026)) would authorize $11.25 billion in bonds: $10 billion for affordable housing and $1.25 billion for a longstandingCalVet home-loan program. (https://veteran.com/start/?src=adw&adg=185122315662&cmp=compterms&desc=calculator&matchtype=p&adid=803809597618&targetid=kwd-297340664879&label=&campaignid=23211217847&extid=&gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=23211217847&gbraid=0AAAAAqq9dHmkha--aWxuqkJFb13gc3lv2&gclid=CjwKCAjwq8PVBhAKEiwA2i3SHZePD1ETl_2tqMBf65xQCzjoSQ7GCNQ3Jj7lr4UZqy9t2I0slreQtBoCALsQAvD_BwE) Funds raised by Prop. 1 would support construction and preservation of affordable apartments (https://www.enterprisecommunity.org/learning-center/resources/2026-california-affordable-housing-production-pipeline?utm_source=chatgpt.com), supportive housing, homeownership assistance, farmworker and tribal housing, student housing and infrastructure needed for affordable developments.
It’s undeniable that Californians struggle with rents they cannot afford, homelessness and home prices that put ownership beyond the reach of many working families.
Private developers generally cannot build housing for low-income and extremely low-income households and charge rents these families can afford while recovering the cost of construction. Every dollar the state invests leverages $4 from federal, local and private funding, according to the California Budget & Policy Center.
And taxpayers wouldn’t be purchasing a fleeting benefit. Affordable apartments receiving these subsidies generally must remain affordable for 55 years. Proponents estimate that turnover during that period could allow roughly 500,000 households to benefit.
There is a cost. TheLegislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/) estimates that repaying the $10 billion housing bond will cost the state’s General Fund $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years — roughly one-quarter of 1% of today’s General Fund budget. The separate $1.25 billion veterans portion is expected to be repaid through veterans’ mortgage payments, as previous CalVet bonds have been.
Opponents rightly say that housing in California is too expensive to build. But their argument that lawmakers should attack those costs instead of subsidizing affordable housing presents a false choice.
California can do both.
In just the past two legislative sessions, for instance, lawmakers have approved a series of changes to speed up environmental reviews and permitting, reduce some impact fees and simplify affordable-housing financing. The state’s newOne-Stop Shop financing reforms (https://ternercenter.berkeley.edu/research-and-policy/california-governors-budget-proposal-advances-a-one-stop-shop-for-affordable-housing/) and impact-fee changes alone are estimated by the Newsom administration to reduce affordable housing costs by $60,000-$70,000 per unit.
Government should eliminate unnecessary expenses, but it cannot eliminate the real costs of roads, schools, water, sewer and other infrastructure communities need as they grow. Nor is government responsible for every rising construction expense. Land, materials, interest rates, insurance, labor, contractor practices and other factors all contribute.
That’s why Proposition 1 should become something more than another infusion of money. California should use this enormous investment to learn precisely why affordable housing costs what it does.
For every project receiving bond money, the state should collect standardized information about land, construction, financing, permit and impact fees, professional services, labor expense, financing sources, approval times and change orders. This would allow researchers to compare similar projects being financed and determine why one costs $450,000 per unit while another costs $800,000 a unit.
And Californians should not have to become government accounting detectives to find the results.
The state should create a simple, prominently displayed public dashboard showing money awarded and spent, units produced and preserved, project locations, costs per unit and completion times. Proponents agreed with us that such transparency is achievable.
That need became obvious when we asked them what measurable results from California’s 2018 housing bond justify returning to voters for substantially more money. They cited strong demand and the fact that its funding was fully committed within five years, but could not readily provide the kind of statewide performance measures voters deserve.
Housing is fundamental to economic mobility. A family struggling to keep a roof over its head has little opportunity to save, educate its children, emphasize wellness or build financial security.
California needs those homes. It also needs to learn how to build the next ones faster and for less.
Proposition 1 gives California (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/proposition-1-californias-veterans-and-affordable-housing-bond/) the opportunity to do better.

October 1, 2026
Dear friends,
I am pleased to submit the 2026 Debt Affordability Report to you, my last one as your State Treasurer and a document required to be sent annu-
ally to provide critical information regarding our general fund-supported bond programs. I am pleased to report that credit rating agencies and
investors alike continue to positively recognize California’s commitments to fiscal responsibility and transparency, demonstrated by our strong and
stable bond ratings and robust demand for our bonds. This recognition is critical to our ability to efficiently raise significant capital to build and
improve critical infrastructure throughout the state, including for housing, schools, roads, and many other projects that benefit our constituents.
My office’s continued commitment to meeting our debt obligations in full and on time has never been stronger and continues to endure across
market and economic cycles, maintaining our state’s market leadership as the benchmark issuer for the broader municipal bond market.
In the past fiscal year, my office expertly executed our state’s debt offerings despite continuing and enhanced volatility driven largely by federal
actions nationally and globally. During a year when inflation continued at over 3 percent, broad tariffs were legally invalidated and then partially re-
imposed, a federal government shutdown eliminated economic data releases for a significant period of time, our country went to war in Iran and a
new Federal Reserve chairman was seated, financial markets were volatile. Despite these major developments, however, artificial intelligence-related
themes continued to support the equity market while the bond market remained relatively stable through much of the fiscal year. However, in
March 2026 interest rates started to trend higher and as I deliver this report to you rates continue to climb, with the 10-year Treasury yield hitting a
20-year high in September. With higher interest rates comes a higher cost to service our debt, which can create other budget impacts and funding
tradeoffs. As a result, continued careful consideration of all legislation and policies that impact our fiscal health will be critical in the years ahead.
California’s overall debt profile remains stable. Our general obligation (GO) bond’s double-A credit ratings were reaffirmed by all three major
rating agencies in 2025-26. The rating agencies continue to cite the State’s large and diverse economic base, healthy liquidity and reserves,
and a stable long-term liability profile as key strengths, while noting ongoing structural challenges such as revenue volatility and exposure to
physical risks such as natural disasters. Our debt portfolio is largely and conservatively comprised of fixed rate debt, with variable rate exposure
maintained well below statutory and policy limits. Affordability indicators—such as debt service relative to general fund revenues and other
measures of leverage—remain within historical norms and continue to reflect the scale and diversity of the State’s economy. However, these
debt load measurements are also higher than many of the most populous states, so issuing debt at levels that significantly outpace economic
and budget growth is likely to erode our current strengths.
During the last fiscal year my office executed the issuance of $7.2 billion of general obligation bonds and $1.4 billion of lease revenue bonds,
all primarily secured by the general fund. Of these amounts, we sold $3.1 billion of refunding bonds that will produce $401 million of debt
service savings to the general fund over the life of the bonds. During my almost 8 years in office, I am proud that we refinanced debt that will
save the state’s general fund over $8.4 billion.
Looking ahead, my office anticipates continued issuance of general fund-supported bonds for both new money and refinancing purposes.
As of June 30, 2026, we have over $44 billion of authorized but unissued bonds, and voters will be asked in November to consider almost
$20 billion of additional general obligation bond authorization. As always, we will execute the sale of such bonds based on prudent financial
management principles in the interest of achieving the lowest cost to finance critical statewide capital investments.
My office stands ready to assist as you consider the State’s existing obligations and future financing needs. Thank you for your continued col-
laboration to manage our state’s debt in a fiscally responsible manner.
In Peace and Friendship,

PREFACE
Government Code Section 12330 requires the State Trea-
surer to submit an annual Debt Affordability Report (DAR)
to the Governor and Legislature. The report must provide
the following information:
• A listing of authorized but unissued debt supported by
the General Fund that the Treasurer intends to sell dur-
ing the current year (2026-27) and the following year
(2027-28), and the projected increase in debt service as
a result of those sales.
• A description of the market for state bonds.
• An analysis of state bonds’ credit ratings.
• A listing of outstanding debt supported by the General
Fund and a schedule of debt service requirements for
the debt.
• A listing of authorized but unissued bonds that would
be supported by the General Fund.
• Identification of pertinent debt ratios, such as debt service
to General Fund revenues, debt to personal income, debt
to estimated full value of property and debt per capita.
• A comparison of the pertinent debt ratios for the state
with those of the 10 most populous states.
• The percentage of the state’s outstanding general ob-
ligation (GO) bonds constituting fixed rate bonds,
variable rate bonds, bonds that have an effective fixed
interest rate through a hedging contract and bonds
that have an effective variable interest rate through a
hedging contract.
• A description of any hedging contract, the outstanding
face value, the effective date, the expiration date, the
name and ratings of the counterparty, the rate or float-
ing index paid by the state and the counterparty, and an
assessment of how the contract met its objectives.
NOTES ON TERMINOLOGY
• This report frequently uses the words “bonds” and “debt”
interchangeably, even when the underlying obligation se-
curing the bonds does not constitute debt subject to limi-
tation under California’s constitution. This conforms to
the municipal market convention that applies the terms
“debt” and “debt service” to a wide variety of fixed in-
come instruments, regardless of their precise legal status.
• The report references fiscal years without using the term
“fiscal year” or “fiscal.” For example, 2026-27 means the
2026-27 fiscal year ending June 30, 2027.

STATE TREASURER’S OFFICE1
California is one of the largest issuers in the $4 trillion U.S.
municipal bond market. Over the last five fiscal years, the
state has issued an average of $7.5 billion of General Obliga-
tion (GO) bonds annually. In 2025-26, the state issued $7.2
billion of GO bonds that were primarily payable from the
general fund. Of that total, $3.3 billion was sold to provide
funding for various voter approved GO bond acts, $784 mil-
lion was sold to retire GO commercial paper, $3.1 billion
was sold to refinance outstanding fixed rate GO bonds to
produce debt service savings, and $55 million was sold to
convert outstanding variable rate GO bonds into fixed rate
GO bonds.
Beyond the issuance of GO bonds and other general fund-
supported debt (the description of which is the subject of
this Debt Affordability Report (DAR) and further described
in subsequent sections), it is important to note that the state
and state-related entities (e.g., Department of Water Re-
sources, California State University System, UC Regents and
others) together issue “billions of dollars” of other types of
debt not supported by the state’s general fund. As a result,
while the state’s GO bond program is one of the single largest
debt programs in the nation, the bonds issued by the broader
universe of California issuers comprise a significant portion
of the overall U.S. municipal bond market every year. This
section focuses on the market for the state’s GO bonds; how-
ever, all state and state-related bond issuers are similarly im-
pacted by the overall bond market described in this section.
The market and price for the state’s GO bonds are influenced
by many factors specific to the state as well as overall condi-
tions in the financial markets. These factors include but are
not limited to the economy, general market interest rates,
significant domestic and global events, national and state
personal income tax rates, the supply of and demand for mu-
nicipal bonds, and investor perception of the state’s credit.
For the 12-month period from July 2025 to June 2026, the
municipal bond market has been influenced, by among other
things, Federal Reserve interest rate cuts, inflation driven in
part by tariffs and higher oil prices, various other economic
indicators, Federal government shutdowns, and important
geopolitical events. These influences on the market have re-
sulted in an uncertain interest rate environment. Overall, in-
terest rates have risen across the yield curve, which has main-
tained a generally upward sloping shape (i.e., higher yields are
generally associated with longer terms per security).
STATE-SPECIFIC FACTORS
One significant state-specific factor in determining the
interest cost of the state’s GO bonds is the credit ratings
assigned by the rating agencies to these bonds. Rating agen-
cies assign credit ratings based on many factors related to
issuers. For the state’s GO bonds, they consider state gov-
ernment revenues, expenditures, reserves, and long-term li-
abilities, as well as the underlying economy of the state. In
addition to the credit ratings, the rating agencies also assign
outlooks to their ratings based on trends that they believe
could lead to rating changes. Investors also consider similar
credit factors in determining their level of participation in
purchasing and holding the state’s GO bonds, which can
affect interest cost on the state’s GO bonds.
How the state handles changes in revenues, which have his-
torically been volatile because the state’s tax revenue system
relies heavily on high-income taxpayers, can impact how the
rating agencies or investors evaluate the state’s credit. When
revenues declined sharply, the state had to implement solu-
tions such as expenditure reductions, delays, fund shifts, and
the use of budget reserves to achieve balanced budgets. For
example, in 2022-23, after a period of unprecedented general
MARKET FOR STATE BONDSSECTION 1
2026 DEBT AFFORDABILITY REPORT2
fund revenue growth, the state faced a severe downturn in
revenues due to a then-declining stock market, high infla-
tion, and rising interest rates. The state declared fiscal emer-
gencies to achieve balanced budgets in its 2024 and 2025
Budget Acts, using a combination of expenditure reductions
and reserve withdrawals. Although revenues and transfers are
forecast to be higher starting in 2027-28, general fund short-
falls were still projected for 2026-27 and 2027-28 absent
further corrective measures. The 2026 Budget Act balanced
the budget using a combination of new revenue solutions,
expenditure reductions, and reserves to help close the short-
falls, while continuing to support critical investments in edu-
cation, mitigating the impacts of climate change, addressing
housing needs, and other important state priorities. Each of
these different types of budget solutions can be viewed differ-
ently from a credit perspective.
Additionally, it is important to note that the 2026 Budget
Act is based on a variety of estimates and assumptions, and
as a result, it faces numerous budgetary and economic risks
with potentially significant general fund impacts. These risks
include, among other things, volatility in the state’s revenues,
threat of an economic recession, significant reductions in fed-
eral funding or other federal actions that could impact the
state’s general fund, adverse decisions in lawsuits against the
state or its related entities, and the cost and persistent un-
funded liabilities related to public employee retirement bene-
fits. These risks are also among the factors that rating agencies
and investors consider in their analysis of the state’s credit.
In 2025-26, the ratings on the state’s GO bonds have re-
mained steady at “AA” by Fitch Ratings (Fitch), “Aa2” by
Moody’s Ratings (Moody’s) and “AA-” by S&P Global Rat-
ings (S&P). In addition, the state’s outlook from each credit
rating agency was “stable” throughout 2025-26.
Notwithstanding the above-mentioned challenges, the
state’s credit spreads have generally improved during 2025-
26. Credit spreads generally represent the difference in yield
between two bonds of similar maturity but different credit
quality. In addition, credit spreads can also change with over-
all interest rates; for municipal bonds, credit spreads tend to
decline as interest rates increase and vice versa. Figure 1 de-
picts the state’s credit spreads, as measured by the difference
between the California GO Municipal Market Data (MMD)
benchmark1 to the national AAA MMD benchmark over the
past decade. The state’s credit spread on its 30-year GO bonds
to the national MMD benchmark has declined from a high of
40 basis points (bps) in September 2022 to a low of negative
six (-6) basis points in June 2026 – the lowest level since 2000.
FACTORS AFFECTING GENERAL BOND MARKETS
Many factors can impact bond markets and interest rates in
general. These factors affect not only the broader U.S. bond
market but also the market for the state’s GO bonds. The
most significant of these factors which impacted bond mar-
kets in 2025-26 included the Federal Open Market Com-

market issuances, the actual borrowing cost achieved by the state generally differs from the levels indicated by the California GO MMD benchmark. Nevertheless, the California GO MMD bench-
mark is a helpful proxy for tracking trends of the state’s GO Bond program’s borrowing cost. The AAA GO MMD benchmark is compiled each day in a similar manner using the GO Bonds of
AAA-rated states. The AAA GO MMD benchmark is generally considered the municipal industry’s benchmark, against which the prices of most new issuances of municipal bonds are compared.

mittee’s adjustments to its target range for the federal funds
rate2, shifting market outlooks on the economy and infla-
tion, speculation about future Federal Reserve and other
central bank actions, full and partial Federal government
shutdowns, concerns about equity prices, and geopolitical
events such as the Iran war. For the municipal bond market
more specifically, there was a significant increase in primary
market issuance supply, which was somewhat balanced by
strong investor demand.
INTEREST RATE TRENDS
In 2025-26, interest rates were comparatively stable versus
prior years by most measures. The relative stability reflected
shifting outlooks about the direction of inflation and the
economy over much of the year. Market participants reacted
to economic data to try to decipher the direction of future
policy actions by the Federal Reserve and other central banks.
When the data reflected higher inflation or a strengthening
economy, interest rates would rise, while lower inflation or
a weakening job market would lead to interest rate declines.
However, the insight from one set of data was often offset by
the next set of data, limiting the extent to which interest rates
changed. Nonetheless, there were several notable phases for
interest rate fluctuations as market sentiments changed.
For the first two months of 2025-26, the Federal Reserve was
maintaining a neutral interest rate policy stance after making
three rate cuts totaling 1 percent in 2024. It was watching the
economy for signs of a slowdown or inflation driven in part
by tariffs, and interest rates held largely steady. As a result,
interest rates generally moved in a narrow band.
Starting in September 2025, a lower court decision strik-
ing down tariffs enacted under the International Emergency
Economic Powers Act, lower inflation numbers, and weaker
economic data all helped to prompt the Federal Reserve to
cut rates by 25 bps in each of three consecutive meetings.
These developments brought about a decline in interest rates.
Interest rates continued to modestly decline as the Federal
government shut down in October 2025 due to a budgetary
impasse. Concerns over the effect of the Federal government
shutdown and the resulting absence of official economic data
continued to keep interest rates relatively low.
When the Federal government reopened, focus turned to
the number of potential rate cuts for 2026; when most
major market strategists priced in only one Federal Reserve
cut, interest rates rose modestly through January.
Then, the nomination of Federal Reserve chairman Warsh,
lower than expected CPI, and the Supreme Court ruling
on tariffs all helped lead to a decline in interest rates in
February 2026.
The U.S. attack of Iran in late February and the resulting
increase in oil prices renewed concerns over inflation and
pushed interest rates higher. Subsequently, news about the
conflict led oil prices and interest rates to fluctuate in the
last months of 2025-26. While outside of 2025-26, in Sep-
tember 2026 the Federal Reserve increased rates by 25 bps
citing the policy action will support a timelier return to the
committee’s 2 percent goal for inflation.

July 2025 through June 2026, as evidenced by changes in

Proposition 1: California’s Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond
A $11.25 Billion Bond to Continue Building Affordable Homes for Californians
July 2026 | By Monica Davalos (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/monica-davalos/)
Print Report
key takeaway
Proposition 1, appearing on the November 2026 ballot, would provide funding for affordable housing and accessible homeownership. Prop. 1 asks voters to authorize a $11.25 billion general obligation bond to fund programs that support the creation and preservation of affordable housing, expand homebuying opportunities for low- and moderate-income Californians and veterans, and invest in permanent solutions to solve homelessness. If Prop. 1 is approved, it would replenish funding for several successful state programs that have exhausted their resources. Prop. 1 was placed on the ballot by the Legislature through passage of Senate Bill 417 (2026) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417).

Over the past six years, California has nearly tripled (https://calhousingpartnership.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/CHP_2026-Housing-Needs-Report-FINAL.pdf) the number of new affordable homes it funds. Yet the state continues to face a severe shortage of affordable housing, particularly for Californians with the lowest incomes. California needs more than 2.5 million new homes, including at least 1 million homes that are affordable to lower-income households. Housing cost pressures fall hardest on California renters as nearly half pay unaffordable rents — a hardship that disproportionately impacts Black and Latinx renters with low incomes, older adults, mixed-status families, and people with disabilities.
Unlike market-rate or luxury housing, affordable housing projects typically cannot be built without subsidies because affordable rents do not generate enough revenue to cover development or operating costs. As a result, affordable housing projects rely on multiple funding streams to close financing gaps. Currently, more than 46,000 affordable homes across California (491 developments) (https://www.enterprisecommunity.org/sites/default/files/2024-04/State_Pipeline_2024_FINAL.pdf) are waiting for the last bit of state funding needed to break ground. Prop. 1 would provide funding for various programs that help bridge the financial gap to keep affordable housing construction moving.
Why Is Affordable Housing Funding Running Out & How Would Prop. 1 Help?
Despite the ongoing housing affordability challenges Californians are facing, state funding for affordable housing has largely disappeared. Over the past several years, affordable housing programs have relied on one-time General Fund investments (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/protecting-progress-state-housing-and-homelessness-funding-must-continue/) to supplement voter-approved housing bonds, but those investments have drastically declined. The 2026 Budget Act only includes one-time investments in two significant affordable housing programs: $500 million for state Low Income Housing Tax Credits and $200 million for the Multifamily Housing Program, effectively leaving multiple programs (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/first-look-understanding-the-governors-proposed-2026-27-california-budget/#h-proposed-budget-includes-no-new-state-funding-for-affordable-housing) without additional funds. Beyond these investments, there is no meaningful ongoing or one-time investment from the state General Fund for affordable housing development.
The state’s remaining modest affordable housing funding sources, including the Affordable Housing and Sustainable Communities Program (AHSC), funded through Cap-and-Invest; state and federal Low-Income Housing Tax Credits; and SB 2 planning funds are insufficient to meet the demand and often require additional funding to be fully leveraged. The AHSC program was expected to receive nearly $800 million per year for affordable housing, but recent changes by the California Air Resources Board put that funding at risk.
Curious About Other Ballot Propositions?
Browse our collection of resources covering California’s statewide ballot measures to help you understand what’s at stake for California this November.
See More Resources (https://calbudgetcenter.org/issues/ballot-propositions/)
The funding approved by voters through the 2018 Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act has been fully committed — exhausted within five years, by the end of 2023, due to overwhelming demand. The state’s flagship Multifamily Housing Program, which relied on funding from the bond and one-time General Fund investments, is routinely oversubscribed by roughly 9 to 1. Together these signal that the barrier to building more affordable housing in California isn’t a lack of will or projects — it’s a lack of sustainable funding.
Without new state investments, affordable housing production will stall just as California is making meaningful progress and as federal cuts threaten to make it even more difficult for Californians to make ends meet, which is why state lawmakers placed Prop. 1 on the ballot.
What Affordable Housing and Homeownership Programs Would Prop. 1 Fund?
Prop. 1 asks voters to authorize $11.25 billion in general obligation (GO) bonds that would support the construction and preservation of affordable rental homes, expand homeownership assistance for low- and moderate-income homebuyers, including veterans, and provide permanent housing for people at risk of or experiencing homelessness. Within these categories, it would provide some funding for programs that serve distinct populations, such as California tribes, farmworkers, unhoused youth, and college students. The bond funds would be allocated as follows:
Affordable Housing Development and Preservation
$5.1 billion for the Multifamily Housing Program (MHP) , which supports the construction, rehabilitation, or preservation of affordable rental housing. At least 10% of units in a MHP development must be available for extremely low-income households who are at the highest risk of facing homelessness. This is one of California’s model affordable housing development programs.
$1.15 billion for supportive housing through the MHP program. Supportive housing provides stable homes with wrap-around services for people who were chronically homeless or at risk of becoming so. These funds can be used for operating subsidy reserves, which are critical to the longevity and sustainability of permanent supportive housing.
Up to 15% — $150 million — would be allocated as grants to acquire or build permanent supportive housing among other specified uses.
Another $150 million is carved out for the capital development or acquisition of youth housing through MHP. This would serve current or former foster youth, homeless minors or youth, or youth at risk of homelessness.
$750 million for the Portfolio Reinvestment Program, which provides funding to rehabilitate and extend the long-term affordability of state-funded rental multifamily housing projects that are at risk of conversion to market-rate housing.
$500 million for the Infill Infrastructure Grant Program . This would provide incentive grants to assist with new construction and rehabilitation of infrastructure that supports high-density affordable and mixed-income housing in locations designated as infill.
$450 million for the Joe Serna, Jr. Farmworker Housing Program to fund grants or loans for the construction or rehabilitation of housing for agricultural employees and their families.
$350 million for affordable student housing projects to be split evenly between the University of California and the California State University.
$200 million for a new Community Anti-Displacement and Preservation Program, which helps protect unsubsidized housing that may naturally be affordable and requires long-term affordability regulations.
$200 million for the Tribal Housing Grant Program which finances housing and housing-related activities to enable tribes to rebuild and reconstitute their communities.
$200 million to the Affordable Housing Innovation Fund for the Local Housing Trust Fund Matching Grant Program. This would fund competitive grants or loans to local housing trust funds that develop, own, lend, or invest in affordable housing and would be used to create pilot programs to demonstrate innovative approaches to creating or preserving affordable housing.
Homeownership
$1.25 billion for the CalVet Home Loan Program (https://www.calvet.ca.gov/HomeLoans) to help veterans and their families purchase homes. This portion of the bond would be repaid through mortgage (principal and interest) payments.
$600 million for the CalHome program. CalHome provides forgivable loans for lower-income households in self-help homeownership projects, including subdivisions and manufactured homes.
$500 million for the My Home downpayment assistance program to fund low-to-moderate income home purchase assistance programs.
What Benefits Would Prop. 1 Create for California’s Economy & Communities?
Prop. 1 would help expand and preserve California’s affordable housing supply while generating economic benefits and advancing the state’s housing goals. The bond would help close the financing gap for affordable rental homes, which serve lower-income California families and include seniors, people with disabilities, farmworkers, college students, and unhoused youth. According to legislative analyses (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417), the bond is expected to:
Produce more than 40,000 new affordable homes for lower-income families and individuals.
Preserve more than 5,500 existing affordable homes , ensuring they remain affordable for future generations.
Create more than 53,000 construction jobs through building new housing across the state.
Generate $1.3 billion in state and local tax revenue that supports local communities and public services.
Every $1 invested in state affordable housing leverages roughly $4 (https://roadmaphome.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/Roadmap-Home-Report-2026.pdf) in federal, local, and private investment, maximizing the impact of public dollars. Affordable housing also delivers economic, health, and environmental benefits (https://affordablehomes.calhousingpartnership.org/). For example:
Children who grow up in affordable housing earn a median of $51,000 more over their lifetimes,
Permanent supportive housing saves an estimated $1.80 in public costs for every $1 invested (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8863642/pdf/nihms-1768403.pdf), and
Building homes near jobs and transit lowers transportation costs while reducing greenhouse gas emissions (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/policy-and-research/intersectional-policy-work/housing-and-climate-change).
Together, these investments would expand housing opportunities, reduce housing instability, strengthen local economies, and help California meet its long-term housing needs.
How Would Prop. 1 Be Repaid?
Prop. 1 asks voters to authorize a total of $11.25 billion in GO bonds, divided as follows:
A $10 billion GO bond for affordable housing and homeownership programs that would be repaid from the state’s General Fund, and
A $1.25 billion veterans’ bond, a type of tax-exempt GO bond, for the CalVet Home Loan program that would be repaid through mortgage payments, with the General Fund as a backstop.
California voters often pass GO bonds to fund infrastructure projects that are designed to serve the public over many generations, as has been the case with affordable housing. Voters have also historically passed veterans’ bonds for CalVet to support homeownership opportunities for veterans.
GO bonds are repaid from the state’s General Fund. Repaying the $10 billion bond would cost $580 million per year for the next 30 years, for a total estimated cost of $17.4 billion ($10 billion in principal and $7.39 billion in interest). As of the governor’s proposed 2026-27 budget, California had $6.3 billion in General Fund debt service for GO bonds, or roughly 2.6% of General Fund expenditures.
In contrast, veterans bonds are generally self-supporting because they are repaid through principal and interest payments made by CalVet Home Loan Program borrowers. However, they are still GO bonds and are ultimately backed by the state’s General Fund. If program revenues were insufficient to cover the debt service, the General Fund would be responsible for the difference. It is unclear how often, if ever, the General Fund has had to backfill debt payments for previous veterans bonds.
Prop. 1 bond dollars would replenish depleted affordable housing programs. But bond dollars alone will not solve the housing shortage, nor would they replace the need for ongoing investments to meet the state’s substantial housing needs.
Prop. 1 and Prop. 38 Draw From Same Bonding Capacity, Face Important Trade Offs
Voters face two GO bond measures on the November 2026 ballot: Prop. 1 and Proposition 38. Prop. 38 would authorize $8.4 billion in GO bonds to support research and development in immunology and immunotherapy. Voters should weigh how each proposal addresses the state’s most pressing needs, fits within California’s limited borrowing capacity, and affects the state’s ability to invest in services that help families today and in the future.
Like all GO bonds, Prop. 38 would require long-term General Fund debt-service payments — estimated at $500 million annually (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-026) for 25 years — reducing budget and bonding capacity for other state priorities. If both Prop. 1 and Prop. 38 are approved, it would reduce General Fund dollars by roughly $1.1 billion annually.
Public sector investment in scientific research is needed, particularly given federal cuts, but Prop. 38 raises important fiscal and policy considerations. GO bonds are conventionally used to finance infrastructure projects — like roads, bridges, or housing — that can be used over decades, roughly matching the time it takes to repay the bond itself.
Funding research through GO bonds does not work the same way. Bond-funded research gets most of the dollars upfront for grants, salaries, and operating costs, but are not guaranteed to be built into a lasting asset. Research findings do compound overtime, but the bond dollars themselves are depleted after a few years. The state then spends years or decades paying interest on bonds that stopped directly funding work long ago. So while scientific research needs funding, a GO bond is not the appropriate funding mechanism. Plus, half of Prop. 38’s funding would be concentrated on a limited set of health conditions, even though California already has multiple public and private research institutions (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-026) conducting work in these areas.
Prop. 1 doesn’t confront these same challenges. While previous affordable housing bond dollars were also used up quickly, they left behind affordable homes that will continue to serve numerous families for decades. Affordable housing developments that use state dollars must have affordability requirements for at least 55 years — way beyond the repayment of the bonds with which they’re financed. The community benefits and capital assets outlast the debt, which is the intended purpose of GO bonds.
Prop. 1 Supporters and Opponents
Prop. 1 is supported by a broad coalition (https://www.housingbondca.com/coalition) of organizations representing housing, business, labor, local government, older adults, tenants, homelessness, urban planning, construction, environmental, and civil rights interests, among others.
Official opposition has been limited. The primary opponents on record include a few Republican state legislators who voted against (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417) placing the measure on the ballot.

Very rich info. Let me note key considerations:

Arguments for YES:
- Severe shortage of affordable housing; 2.2M low-income households competing for 664K affordable rentals; state needs ~1M affordable units by 2031.
- Existing programs (MHP) exhausted 2018 bond funds by end of 2023; MHP oversubscribed 9:1; ~40,000-46,000 pipeline units awaiting final gap funding.
- Bond would subsidize up to 40,000 multifamily units + 2,500 farmworker + 1,200 student beds + help 40,000 households with homeownership (incl. 2,100 vets).
- Cost $500-600M/yr for ~25 years = ~0.25% of General Fund; affordable homes have 55-year affordability covenants — asset life exceeds debt repayment (classic intergenerational equity rationale for capital debt).
- CalVet portion ($1.25B) is self-supporting — no direct general fund cost.
- Leverages ~$4 of federal/local/private for every $1 state.
- Recent reforms (CEQA infill exemption, transit streamlining, one-stop-shop financing, impact fee reduction) reduce per-unit costs by $60-70K, improving ROI vs. 2018 bond.
- Broad support: Governor, Democratic Party, housing groups, labor, veterans groups, local governments, Sacramento Bee, SF Chronicle, KQED? (KQED just reports).
- No organized opposition campaign; no contributions to a No committee; no argument against filed in the official guide.

Arguments for NO:
- State faces structural deficits of $20-35 billion annually; existing debt service $6-8 billion/year; $44 billion authorized-but-unissued bonds; adding $500-600M/yr for 25 years crowds out other spending.
- Total repayment ~$17.4B ($7.4B interest), 15% more in real terms than paying cash.
- Rising interest rates (10-year Treasury at 20-year high in Sept 2026), so borrowing cost may be higher than assumed.
- Debt-service-to-revenue ratio 3.41% → 3.83%, and Prop 1 + Prop 38 together would add ~$1.1B/yr.
- Doesn't address root cause: high construction costs (RAND: subsidized housing costs 1.5x market-rate in CA; local fees, above-market wages).
- Only ~4% of the 1M needed affordable units; drop in the bucket.
- Title criticized as bait-and-switch ("veterans" only ~11% of funds).
- Weak accountability: annual report but no independent audit for most funds; Press Democrat says "housing money without accountability"; Sacramento Bee says proponents couldn't provide performance measures for 2018 bond results.
- Down payment assistance without adding supply could push prices up (Press Democrat's argument).
- Preservation/acquisition of existing apartments adds no new units.
- Media opposition: Mercury News/East Bay Times, LA Daily News/Press-Telegram/OC Register/San Gabriel Valley Tribune, San Diego Union-Tribune, Press Democrat, LA Times columnist George Skelton.
- Media support: Sacramento Bee, SF Chronicle. LA Times editorial board: no position found.
- Hoover Institution leans skeptical (free-market framing).

Weighing: Which is "better"? The question asks for a decision. Let me consider what most evidence-based analyses conclude.

The benefit: ~40,000+ affordable homes with 55-year affordability, which is a long-lived capital asset — the standard economic justification for debt financing. Interest cost is 15% higher in real terms, which is a modest premium for a 55-year asset financed over 25 years.

The "no reform" critique is weakened by the fact that California has recently passed substantial housing reform (CEQA exemption for infill, transit streamlining, one-stop-shop financing consolidation, impact fee reductions) estimated to cut costs $60-70K/unit. Accountability concerns: Prop 1 does include reporting requirements. Let me check the actual text for accountability provisions — annual reports, audits. The Press Democrat says "no independent audit on most of it." Let me verify by checking the SB 417 text provisions.

Also, importantly: does the measure have a "no new taxes" claim? Yes, it's paid from the general fund.

Another consideration: opportunity cost — if it fails, programs stay exhausted, and pipeline projects stall. That's a real harm to low-income households.

Counter-consideration: the state could fund affordable housing from the general fund in surplus years rather than borrowing. But given deficits, that's unlikely.

Let me check the accountability provisions in the bill text and also see if there's any notable analysis of per-unit cost efficiency (e.g., $500K+/unit in CA; $10B/40,000 units = $250K per unit subsidy, which is reasonable given total dev costs of $500-800K/unit).

Let me quickly check the bill text for accountability/reporting and any sunset provisions. Also, check whether the CalVet bond portion has any risk of default costs.

Let me also verify whether there's anything problematic like funds being available to projects without cost controls.

LEGISLATIVE COUNSEL'S DIGEST
SB 417, Limón.
The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026.
Under existing law, there are programs providing assistance for, among other things, emergency housing, multifamily housing, farmworker housing, home ownership for very low and low-income households, and downpayment assistance for first-time home buyers. Existing law also authorizes the issuance of bonds in specified amounts pursuant to the State General Obligation Bond Law and requires that proceeds from the sale of these bonds be used to finance various existing housing programs, capital outlay related to infill development, brownfield cleanup that promotes infill development, and housing-related parks. Existing law, the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2018, authorized, the issuance of bonds in the amount of $4,000,000,000 to finance various existing housing programs, as well as infill infrastructure financing and affordable housing matching grant
programs, as well as financing for a specified program for farm, home, and mobilehome purchase assistance for veterans, pursuant to the State General Obligation Bond Law.
This bill would enact the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026, which, if adopted, would authorize the issuance of bonds in the amount of
$11,250,000,000, pursuant to the State General Obligation Bond Law. Of the proceeds from the sale of these bonds, $10,000,000,000 would be used to finance programs to fund affordable rental housing and home ownership programs, including, among others, the Multifamily Housing Program, the CalHome Program, and the Joe Serna, Jr. Farmworker Housing Grant Program, and $1,250,000,000 would be used to provide additional
funding for the above-described program for farm, home, and mobilehome purchase assistance for veterans, as provided.
This bill would provide for submission of the bond act to the voters at the November 3, 2026, statewide general election, in accordance with specified law.
This bill would declare that it is to take effect immediately as an urgency statute.

The people of the State of California do enact as follows:
SECTION 1.
This act shall be known, and may be cited, as the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026.
SEC. 2.
Part 16.1 (commencing with Section 54050) is added to Division 31 of the Health and Safety Code, to read:
PART 16.1. Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026
CHAPTER
1. General Provisions
54050.
Together with Article 5ab (commencing with Section 998.750) of Chapter 6 of Division 4 of the Military and Veterans Code, this part shall be known, and may be cited, as the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026.
54051.
This part shall only become operative upon adoption by the voters at the November 3, 2026, statewide general election.
54052.
For purposes of this part, “fund” means the Affordable Housing Bond Act Trust Fund of 2026 created pursuant to Section 54054.
CHAPTER
2. Affordable Housing Bond Act Trust Fund of 2026 and Program
54054.
(a) The Affordable Housing Bond Act Trust Fund of 2026 is hereby created within the State Treasury. It is the intent of the Legislature that the proceeds of bonds issued and sold pursuant to this part, exclusive of refunding bonds issued pursuant to Section 54076, be deposited into the fund and used to fund affordable rental housing and home ownership
programs as described in this chapter.
(b) The proceeds of bonds issued and sold pursuant to this part for the purposes specified in this chapter shall be allocated in the following manner:
(1) Five billion one hundred million dollars ($5,100,000,000) to be deposited
into the Housing Rehabilitation Loan Fund established pursuant to Section 50661 to be used for the Multifamily Housing Program authorized by Chapter 6.7 (commencing with Section 50675) of Part
2. At least 10 percent of assisted units in each development receiving these funds shall be affordable to extremely low income households.
(2) One billion one hundred fifty million dollars ($1,150,000,000) to be deposited
into the Housing Rehabilitation Loan Fund established pursuant to Section 50661 to be used for supportive housing, as described in Section 50675.14, pursuant to the Multifamily Housing Program authorized by Chapter 6.7 (commencing with Section 50675) of Part 2. The administering entity shall offer capitalized operating subsidy reserves for supportive housing units in developments receiving these funds.

By Editorial Board (https://www.sonomanews.com/author/editorial-board/)

Props. 1 and 38 would take the state deeper in debt for uncertain gains
Two measures on the November ballot ask voters to borrow $20 billion combined. Proposition 1 would fund housing programs. Proposition 38 would fund immunology research. We recommend a no vote on each.
The state already carries a heavy debt load. California owed about $70 billion on general obligation bonds as of Sept. 1, according to the state treasurer. Voters and lawmakers have authorized nearly $38 billion more in bonds that have not yet been sold.
The bondholders who lent the state money expect to be paid back with interest. The state spends about $6 billion annually from the general fund repaying bonds. Props. 1 and 38 would add roughly $1 billion to that for 20 to 25 years.
When state revenue comes up short, lawmakers can reduce spending or at least slow spending growth. Bond payments, however, are a legal obligation that comes due regardless. Every dollar locked into debt service is a taxpayer dollar unavailable for schools, health care or wildfire protection in a lean year.
Prop. 1: Housing money without accountability
California needs more housing, and Prop. 1 would throw $11.25 billion at the problem without addressing the underlying causes of the state’s housing shortage and high costs. Lawmakers took the easy route. Rather than pass controversial reforms or find money in the budget, they chose to ask voters to borrow.
Most of the money, about $7.2 billion, would pay for building, buying and rehabilitating multifamily rental housing, affordable housing and supportive housing for the homeless. Smaller pools of money totaling about $2.3 billion would provide mortgage and down-payment assistance.
Giving buyers more money with which to bid without adding homes would push prices higher. And buying existing apartments does not add a single home to ease market pressure.
The measure also lacks accountability. It calls for an annual report on how well things are going, but there is no independent audit on most of it and no remedy if the return on investment is lackluster. There also are no plans for when the money runs out and no guarantee that lawmakers will not meddle and reapportion the funds.
Californians have cause for skepticism that the state will spend this housing money well. A 2024 state audit found that California had not consistently tracked whether its homelessness spending worked. Sacramento should prove that it can measure and deliver results before asking for bonds that will cost taxpayers $500 million to $600 million per year.
Prop. 38: Science by ballot box
Immunology and immunotherapy hold real promise, but Prop. 38 is the wrong way to fund research into them. Only one University of California-affiliated institute appears to qualify for half of the money, according to a CalMatters analysis. Coincidentally, that institute’s co-founder is one of Prop. 38’s biggest backers.
One problem with this approach is that state law would lock in how the money could be spent. Research dollars should support the centers with the most promising results and best scientists. Maybe that is the UC affiliate now, but that could change.
Bonds also fit research poorly. They are better suited to bridges and schools that last decades than to research that might never bear fruit. Even if there are commercial breakthroughs, the Legislative Analyst’s Office says royalties could take decades to repay the bonds, if they ever do.
Medical research is a legitimate state interest. If California wants to fund it, the state ought to do so through the regular budget process, weighing its value against other state priorities, not with a special bond that will cost taxpayers $500 million to $600 million per year.
You can email letters to the editor to letters@pressdemocrat.com (mailto:letters@pressdemocrat.com). Don’t miss The Press Democrat’s new weekly opinion newsletter, Second Thoughts. Sign up here (https://signups.medianewsgroup.com/press_democrat_second_thoughts).
